Program: The PIER – Port Innovation, Engagement & Research
Description: The PIER is a supply-chain and ocean gateway innovation hub at the Halifax Seaport that provides flexible co-working, meeting rooms, and testbeds for logistics, shipping, port-tech, and marine-related firms. By clustering shippers, carriers, tech vendors, researchers, and workforce partners in one space, it operates as a sector-specific pod that breaks down silos and speeds up solution development and vendor–employer connections. This coordinated environment increases high-quality roles and a...
Challenge: Thin job density and limited career ladders
Solution: Co-working Spaces with Sector 'Pods': Develop affordable co-working facilities that include sector-specific pods (tech, creative, trades-adjacent services) to concentrate talent, foster collaboration and accelerate company growth into multi-role employers.

Description: Shannex provides scholarships and education support for students in programs like Continuing Care Assistant (CCA), Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN), and Registered Nurse (RN). Awards typically include a commitment to work at Shannex communities in Nova Scotia for a set term after graduation, giving learners a funded path into local, in-demand roles and a clear on-ramp to career ladders in seniors’ care.
Challenge: Thin job density and limited career ladders
Solution: Local Talent Scholarships with Return-to-Service: Fund scholarships (post-secondary or technical) that include agreements or incentives for recipients to work in the community for a defined period, creating predictable pipelines into local career ladders.
Address: 100 Baker Drive, Suite 200, Dartmouth, NS B2W 4M1

Program: KBRS/Meridia Atlantic Canada Salary Guides & Job Board
Organization: KBRS (Knightsbridge Robertson Surrette) / Meridia Recruitment Solutions
Description: KBRS and its recruitment division Meridia publish anonymized Atlantic Canada salary guides and role-specific compensation studies drawing on employer surveys and placement data, with Halifax/Nova Scotia benchmarks to compare against wider Canadian norms. They also maintain a regional job board for professional and executive roles, often including pay bands, to improve transparency and support fair, market-aligned negotiations.
Challenge: Wage competitiveness versus rising living costs
Solution: Local Salary Benchmarking and Transparency Hub: Run a community-managed, anonymized salary benchmarking service and jobs board so local employers and jobseekers can compare compensation against national/Provincial norms and negotiate fairer pay.
Address: Suite 1800, Purdy’s Wharf Tower II, 1969 Upper Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3R7

Description: A parent-run, non-profit cooperative preschool in Halifax’s North End where member families share governance and volunteer classroom support to keep fees affordable. By pooling parent time and resources, the co-op expands access to early learning and childcare hours, helping young parents balance work or study with dependable, community-based care.
Challenge: Wage competitiveness versus rising living costs
Solution: Community Childcare Cooperatives: Establish parent-run or worker cooperative childcare programs that reduce fees, increase availability, and enable more young parents to participate in the workforce.

Organization: Sackville Heights Cooperative Nursery School Society
Description: A community-based, parent-governed cooperative nursery school offering play-based early learning with family volunteer participation to reduce operating costs and tuition. The co-op model increases local childcare availability and helps parents remain in or return to the workforce by providing reliable, affordable part-day care within the community centre.
Challenge: Wage competitiveness versus rising living costs
Solution: Community Childcare Cooperatives: Establish parent-run or worker cooperative childcare programs that reduce fees, increase availability, and enable more young parents to participate in the workforce.
Address: 45 Connolly Road, Lower Sackville, NS B4E 1S8

Description: Hire Me Halifax is a recurring hiring event where students, recent graduates, and newcomers pitch their skills to local employers, followed by rapid networking and on-the-spot interview opportunities. The program includes short prep workshops (pitch building, resume and LinkedIn tune-ups) and connects candidates to immediate roles, internships, and project placements across sectors.
Solution: Local Hiring & Skills Fair Series: Host regular themed hiring fairs and micro-workshops (trades week, tech week, arts & culture week) where employers commit to on-the-spot interviews, short trials and co-op offers targeted to youth and newcomers.
Address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

Description: StFX’s Alumni Association offers an online alumni community and directory, along with active Nova Scotia chapters that host regular gatherings and professional networking events. Alumni volunteer as mentors and speakers to support students and recent graduates, share job leads, and keep the Antigonish community ties strong—facilitating pathways for StFX grads who wish to return to or remain in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Local Alumni Network & Directory: Create a community-run digital directory and regular meetup series for local alumni (students, former workers, emigrants) to stay connected, share job leads, mentor youth, and coordinate return initiatives.

Program: Feed Nova Scotia Food Distribution Network
Description: Feed Nova Scotia operates a province-wide consolidation and distribution hub that receives large volumes of donated food at its Dartmouth warehouse. It packs and ships pallets and totes on scheduled routes to more than 140 member food banks and meal programs, which then coordinate local pickup times and volunteer-supported last-mile distribution to residents. The centralized hub and route scheduling reduce transportation costs for community agencies and ensure consistent, consolidated deliver...
Solution: Community Freight and Consolidation Hub: Set up a local consolidation point for deliveries and bulk orders to lower shipping costs for businesses and residents. Organize coordinated delivery days, group purchasing to reduce frequency and price of long-distance freight, and a volunteer driver pool for last-mile distribution.

Description: The Canadian Red Cross delivers Psychological First Aid training that equips community members, volunteers, educators, and employers to recognize signs of distress and mental-health crises, provide calm, supportive initial assistance, and connect individuals to professional and community resources. Courses are offered in person and online across Nova Scotia, making practical skills like active listening, safety planning, and referral pathways accessible to residents and workplaces.
Solution: Community mental-health first aid training: Regular, subsidized training sessions teach residents, youth workers, teachers, and employers how to recognize crises, provide initial support, and connect people to professional services.

Program: Students and New Grads – Clinical Placements and Employment Pathways
Description: Shannex partners with Nova Scotia institutions (e.g., NSCC, Dalhousie, CBU) to host practicums and co‑ops for nursing, continuing care, and allied health learners in long‑term care and home care settings across the province. The program provides preceptors, structured mentorship, scholarships, and clear pathways to local employment, encouraging students to remain in Nova Scotia communities after graduation.
Solution: Healthcare student placement and retention partnerships: Community groups collaborate with regional colleges and universities to host clinical placements, offer homestays, and create mentorship and incentive packages that encourage new graduates to stay or return.
Address: 261 Joseph Zatzman Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1M7

Description: Good2Talk provides 24/7 phone and text support for post-secondary students in Nova Scotia, offering immediate, non-clinical crisis support and problem-solving. Using professional counsellors and trained volunteer crisis responders (for text), the service offers short-term respite and connects students to campus services, community mental-health resources, and provincial crisis supports as needed.
Solution: Crisis respite and tele-response volunteer program: A volunteer-staffed crisis respite and phone/video check-in program offers short-term, non-clinical support during mental-health crises and connects callers to professional services as needed.
Address: 439 University Avenue, Suite 300, Toronto, ON M5G 1Y8

Program: Alderney Landing Farmers’ Market & Pop-Up Vendor Program
Description: Located in a municipally connected cultural facility, Alderney Landing hosts weekly and seasonal markets that offer affordable, short-term vendor tables and pop-up retail booths for small businesses and artisans. These temporary spaces reduce overhead and provide immediate customer exposure, often serving as a launchpad toward permanent storefronts.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Pop-up Incubators and Shared Workspaces: Use vacant storefronts, municipal buildings, or school facilities to host temporary co-working hubs and pop-up shops that reduce rent barriers, provide short-term affordable space, and expose entrepreneurs to customers and mentors.

Description: CNIB’s Halifax team provides on-site accessibility assessments and advisory services for public buildings and small businesses using recognized standards (e.g., CSA, CNIB’s Clearing Our Path). They train staff and volunteers on inclusive customer service and wayfinding and deliver actionable audit reports that prioritize fixes like tactile signage, lighting/contrast improvements, and hearing assistive technologies. CNIB also advises clients on leveraging Nova Scotia grant programs (e.g., Acce...
Solution: Community Accessibility Audits and Micro-Grants: Train local volunteers to run accessibility audits for public buildings and small businesses, and provide community micro-grants to implement priority accessibility upgrades (ramps, signage, hearing loops).

Description: CNIB’s Come to Work program partners with employers who commit to accessible, inclusive hiring for people who are blind, Deafblind, or have low vision. The program helps employers remove biased job requirements, conduct accessibility reviews, and implement accommodations throughout recruitment and onboarding, while training HR teams on inclusive practices. Participating employers are recognized through CNIB’s networks and events, signalling a public, community-backed commitment to accessibili...
Solution: Inclusive Hiring Pledges for Local Employers: Create a community-backed pledge program that helps small and medium employers adopt inclusive hiring practices, remove biased job requirements, embed accessibility accommodations, and display a public commitment to equity.

Description: CNIB’s Come to Work program supports job seekers with sight loss through resume and interview coaching, job matching, and mentorship. It also runs accessible technology training and demonstrations (e.g., screen readers, magnification, and workplace accessibility tools) to prepare candidates and advise employers on effective accommodations. The team regularly engages employers through information sessions and roundtables to improve inclusive hiring and retention practices.
Solution: Disability Employment Support and Skills Labs: Host community-run skills labs offering resume help, workplace accommodation planning, assistive tech demos, and employer roundtables to improve hiring and retention of people with disabilities.

Description: Halifax Port Authority’s Supplier Diversity Program encourages participation and spending with underrepresented businesses in the Port’s procurement and capital projects. Through targeted outreach, inclusive vendor registration, and social value criteria for tenders, the Port increases opportunities for Mi’kmaq-led, African Nova Scotian, newcomer-owned, 2SLGBTQ+-led, and disability-run firms, and encourages prime contractors to allocate a share of subcontracts to these suppliers.
Solution: Local Procurement Equity Initiative: Encourage municipal and institutional procurement policies that earmark a percentage of contracts for Mi'kmaq-led, African Nova Scotian, newcomer-owned, 2SLGBTQ+-led, and disability-run businesses and co-ops.

Description: ArtsSmarts Nova Scotia funds collaborative artist–teacher projects in K–12 schools across the province, supporting short-term residencies where artists co-plan curriculum-linked activities and lead hands-on workshops with students. Projects commonly culminate in public showcases—exhibitions, performances, or installations—co-created by youth, building creative skills and confidence. The microgrant model encourages cost-sharing with school budgets, parent/guardian councils, and community partn...
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
Solution: Artist-in-School and Community Residency Programs: Partner schools, libraries, and community centres with artists for temporary residencies that deliver workshops, co-created public works, and skill-building for youth. Funding comes from microgrants, parent councils, and local foundations.
Address: 1741 Brunswick Street, 3rd Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 3X8

Description: Ticket Halifax is a locally run ticketing and event-listing platform where artists and arts organizations can promote shows, readings, classes, and festivals and sell tickets directly to audiences. Integrated with The Coast’s local media channels, it provides strong regional promotion and artist-friendly tools, helping creatives reach new attendees. Organizers receive sales and attendance reports they can use to make data-informed programming and scheduling decisions.
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
Solution: Digital Platform for Local Creatives: A community-managed online marketplace and events calendar where artists sell work, list classes, and promote shows. Low fees and local promotion increase reach and provide data to inform programming decisions.

Description: The Canadian Red Cross delivers emergency preparedness education to Nova Scotia schools and youth groups, including workshops, drills, and training on severe weather, flooding, and power outages. Youth practice creating family emergency plans and kits and learn response skills (first aid and community readiness) that strengthen local resilience to climate-related disasters.
Solution: Youth engagement and resilience education: Schools and youth groups run hands-on programs (shoreline restoration, emergency drills, green trades apprenticeships) to build skills and retention of young residents.

Program: St. Francis Xavier University Biomass District Heating Upgrade
Description: StFX added a biomass boiler to its central heating plant and distributes steam/hot water through an on‑campus network to multiple buildings, creating a campus‑scale district energy system. The project leverages locally sourced biomass to displace electric and oil heating, cutting energy costs and peak grid demand while using a shared thermal backbone.
Solution: District heating and shared thermal systems: Develop small-scale district heating (biomass, waste heat recovery, geo) in dense communities or industrial parks to reduce reliance on electrical heating, lower per‑unit energy costs and capture local fuel resources.

Description: FEED Nova Scotia centrally raises funds, manages donor receipting, and distributes resources and training to a network of small, community-based food banks and meal programs. This shared platform reduces the administrative and fundraising burden on local agencies—many volunteer-run—so they can focus on frontline food security work while benefiting from coordinated grants, logistics, and capacity-building.
Solution: Shared Administrative Services: Develop a shared-services hub offering pooled accounting, fundraising, HR, and grant-writing support for small nonprofits to reduce overhead, professionalize operations, and free frontline staff for mission work.

Description: Feed Nova Scotia partners with employers to run workplace giving campaigns, corporate fund and food drives, and group volunteer shifts in its Dartmouth warehouse. Companies also contribute in‑kind logistics support, pro bono services, and sponsorships that help strengthen distribution systems and training for the network of food banks and meal programs across the province. This coordinated business–community approach boosts nonprofit capacity and stabilizes essential social supports for famil...
Solution: Business–Community Partnership Network: Organize a local employer network for in-kind support, payroll-giving, pro bono services, employee volunteer days, and sponsorship of capacity-building efforts for nonprofits.

Description: Scouting in Nova Scotia engages youth in leadership, outdoor skills, and community projects supported by trained adult Scouters, many of whom are older residents and retirees. Intergenerational teams plan and deliver service activities, skill workshops, and youth-led governance within local groups and councils. By mobilizing seasoned volunteers alongside young people, the program transfers skills and strengthens the volunteer base of community organizations across the province.
Solution: Intergenerational Mentorship Circles: Establish mentorship programs pairing older residents and retirees with young people to transfer skills, support projects, and share organizational leadership, while expanding volunteer capacity.

Description: Feed Nova Scotia’s annual Stuff‑A‑Bus campaign, delivered in partnership with Halifax Transit, mobilizes volunteers at buses, transit terminals, and grocery stores for a festive food and fund drive that engages the wider public. The high‑visibility event combines donor drives with hands‑on volunteer participation and public celebration of community contributions, aligning with the model of an annual community giving and volunteer festival.
Solution: Annual Community Giving and Volunteer Festivals: Organize yearly festivals that combine volunteer recruitment, donor drives, recognition ceremonies, and mini-grants to energize philanthropy and celebrate community contributions.

Organization: University of King's College School of Journalism
Description: The Signal is the University of King’s College School of Journalism’s multimedia news site and podcast, publishing in-depth profiles and features from across Halifax and Nova Scotia. Student journalists produce short videos, audio features, and social content that elevate the stories of local entrepreneurs, artists, and community builders, often picked up and shared through wider local media channels. By training new storytellers and continuously surfacing compelling, solutions-focused narrat...
Solution: Community Storytelling Campaign: Collect and amplify local success stories (entrepreneurs, artists, tradespeople, returnees) through short videos, podcasts, social posts and local media to reshape narratives about opportunity and quality of life. Volunteer storytellers, schools, and community media can produce content and host listening events.

Program: Alderney Landing Farmers’ Market & Community Events
Organization: Alderney Landing Community Cultural Centre Society
Description: Alderney Landing activates the Dartmouth waterfront with year-round farmers’ markets, seasonal night markets, outdoor concerts, and festivals like Christkindlmarket and Canada Day celebrations. These pop-up markets and street-festival-style events animate public plazas and the ferry terminal area, drawing residents and visitors into shared spaces that showcase local culture, vendors, and civic pride.
Solution: Neighborhood Place-Making Projects: Mobilize residents to improve public spaces (murals, park upgrades, pop-up markets, street festivals) that make communities more attractive, visible and newsworthy while demonstrating civic pride and livability.

Description: Evergreen Festival is a multi-week celebration on the Halifax waterfront featuring free outdoor concerts, light art installations, cultural performances, and local markets. Produced by Build Nova Scotia, it expands seasonal programming with creative showcases that spotlight local artists and businesses, attracting residents and visitors while generating positive media coverage for Nova Scotia’s lifestyle and culture.
Solution: Cultural Festivals & Creative Showcases: Expand and promote festivals and arts events that highlight local culture, talent and lifestyle—run volunteer-led pop-up concerts, gallery nights, food trails and heritage tours to attract visitors and media.
Address: 1875 Upper Water Street, Suite 301, Halifax, NS B3J 1S9

Description: The Port of Halifax engages trained volunteer ambassadors to greet cruise passengers and other visitors at the Halifax Seaport, offering wayfinding, local recommendations, and curated walking routes. By serving as friendly hosts—and often supporting media and travel trade familiarization visits—these volunteers create authentic local connections that enhance Nova Scotia’s image and encourage return visits and investment.
Solution: Neighbourhood Hospitality & Host Programs: Train volunteers from across the community to serve as 'hosts' for visiting journalists, prospective investors, students and job candidates—offering authentic local tours, introductions and hospitality that change perceptions.

Program: NSCC Career and Employment Services – Career Fairs & Employer Showcases
Description: Across NSCC campuses, Career and Employment Services runs themed career fairs and employer showcases (e.g., trades, ICT, health) where recruiters provide on-the-spot interviews, co-op recruitment, and apprenticeship sign-ups for students and recent grads. Events are paired with micro-workshops like portfolio reviews, interview prep, and credential/skills mapping to ensure alignment between training and employer needs.
Solution: Local Hiring & Skills Fair Series: Host regular themed hiring fairs and micro-workshops (trades week, tech week, arts & culture week) where employers commit to on-the-spot interviews, short trials and co-op offers targeted to youth and newcomers.

Program: Student and Graduate Employment (NSCC Job Matching)
Description: NSCC’s Student and Graduate Employment service runs a province-wide job board and matching support for NSCC students and alumni. Employers post apprenticeship, seasonal, contract, and short project roles, and graduates create profiles so their skills can be quickly matched to local industry needs. NSCC also conducts graduate follow-up surveys that track employment and mobility, informing efforts to re-engage alumni who plan to return to Nova Scotia.
Solution: Alumni-to-Employer Matching Platform: Build a lightweight local platform to match alumni skills with employer needs, track return intentions, and advertise short-term project or contract work to ease re-entry.

Program: Mental Health First Aid (MHFA) – Continuing Education
Description: NSCC’s Continuing Education regularly hosts Mental Health First Aid courses (including Standard and Adults Who Interact with Youth) at campuses and online, training teachers, youth workers, employers, and community members to recognize symptoms, respond safely, and connect individuals to professional care and community resources. By integrating MHFA into accessible, short-format offerings, NSCC expands practical crisis-recognition and referral skills across Nova Scotia’s communities and workp...
Solution: Community mental-health first aid training: Regular, subsidized training sessions teach residents, youth workers, teachers, and employers how to recognize crises, provide initial support, and connect people to professional services.

Description: This NSCC program trains students in marine sensors, data systems, robotics/ROVs, and field operations for ocean industries, with applied research and industry work placements. Graduates support innovation in aquaculture, marine environmental monitoring, and coastal infrastructure, and many roles can be performed in distributed or digital-first teams. The program builds in-demand technical talent that enables blue-economy growth and diversifies employment opportunities in coastal communities.
Solution: Diversify coastal livelihoods and skills training: Offer local training and startup support for aquaculture, green trades, ecotourism, and digital/remote work to reduce economic reliance on vulnerable resource sectors.

Description: NSCC publicly reports graduate employment rates, time-to-employment, in-province employment retention, and wage outcomes by program and campus through its graduate outcomes reporting. These transparent results showcase local talent success and the share of graduates working in Nova Scotia, providing communities and employers with concrete metrics to counter perceptions of limited opportunity and to celebrate workforce wins.
Solution: Transparent Local Data & Success Dashboard: Assemble community-collected metrics—job openings filled locally, new businesses launched, retention rates, wages—and publish a local 'progress dashboard' to counter myths with facts and celebrate wins publicly.

Description: IGNITE operates rural innovation hubs that host free clinics, office hours, and workshops with legal, accounting, and marketing partners to support early-stage founders, many of whom are youth. Working with Invest Nova Scotia and regional partners, IGNITE also helps deliver funding opportunities such as Spark (non-dilutive microgrants), enabling young entrepreneurs to launch and scale companies that create local jobs.
Challenge: Thin job density and limited career ladders
Solution: Youth Entrepreneurship Microgrants and Clinics: Offer small start-up grants plus free legal, accounting and marketing clinics through community partners to help young entrepreneurs create scalable businesses that can hire locally as they grow.

Program: IGNITE Rural Pitch Competitions and Demo Nights
Description: IGNITE Atlantic organizes regular community pitch events and program demo nights across its rural hubs, giving founders from Western and Northern Nova Scotia opportunities to present to local investors, buyers, and ecosystem partners. These gatherings often feature networking and community showcases at the Yarmouth and New Glasgow hubs, creating immediate pathways for customer introductions, pilot sign-ups, and local sales.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Regular Pitch Nights and Demo Days: Host monthly or quarterly community pitch events where founders present to local investors, customers, and service providers; combine with 'buy local' showcases to generate feedback, visibility, and immediate sales opportunities.

Description: IGNITE Atlantic spotlights founders, students, and innovators from rural Nova Scotia through articles, videos, and events that celebrate homegrown success. By telling the journeys of local companies and youth-led projects—and pointing to ecosystem supports that helped them—IGNITE’s storytelling inspires students and returnees to pursue careers and startups in their home communities and fosters cross-sector collaboration.
Solution: Local Success Stories Campaign: Promote returning and staying talent by storytelling—sharing profiles of local entrepreneurs, apprentices, and innovators to inspire youth and signal that viable careers can be built here.
Address: 208 Main Street, Unit 101, Yarmouth, NS B5A 1C8

Program: IGNITE Atlantic Industry Nights & Career Showcases
Description: IGNITE Atlantic convenes recurring Industry Nights, open houses, and youth career showcases at its innovation hubs, bringing local businesses, trades, oceans, and agri-food companies together with students and job seekers. Employers present what they do, share apprenticeship and internship opportunities, and connect directly with participants—making rural Nova Scotia career pathways visible and attainable.
Solution: Local Business & Career Showcases: Host regular open-house events that let local businesses, trades, and creative enterprises present career pathways, apprenticeships and internships to high-school and post-secondary students and job-seekers, making pathways and growth visible.

Program: Halifax Affordable Access Program (Recreation, Camps and After-School)
Description: The municipality’s Affordable Access Program provides income-based discounts—up to full subsidy—for recreation programming delivered at community-run centres, including day camps and some before/after-school childcare options. This transparent sliding-scale model reduces or eliminates fees for low-income families, with the municipality underwriting discounts and community partners supporting access through ongoing fundraising.
Solution: Flexible Fee Models and Sliding-scale Policies: Community-run centres adopt transparent sliding-scale fee structures, sibling discounts and pay-what-you-can days, supported by local fundraising to sustain operations while increasing affordability.

Program: Halifax Regional Municipality Procurement (Supplier Engagement & Tenders)
Description: HRM’s Procurement division posts public tenders and runs supplier engagement such as 'How to Do Business with HRM' sessions and reverse trade shows to help local SMEs navigate municipal purchasing. Through social value and community-benefit practices, it encourages participation from local and diverse suppliers and connects them with procurement opportunities, advancing buy-local outcomes in public spending.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Community Procurement and 'Buy Local' Pledges: Mobilize institutions, non-profits, and residents to commit to buying from local startups and small businesses; coordinate procurement opportunities and procurement-ready training for local suppliers.

Program: Cultural Festivals and Events Funding Program
Description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s grant program provides operating and project funding to non-profit organizers of public cultural festivals and events across HRM. Its assessment criteria emphasize diversity, accessibility, and inclusion, which channels sponsorship to festivals that feature and are led by Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, 2SLGBTQ+, and disabled artists, creating neighborhood-based, cross-cultural engagement.
Solution: Local Inclusive Festivals and Arts Grants: Sponsor neighborhood festivals and small grants that prioritize programming by Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, 2SLGBTQ+, and disabled artists to celebrate diversity and create cross-cultural engagement.

Description: HRM’s land-use rules enable secondary and backyard suites by-right in many zones, making it easier for homeowners to add small rental units on existing properties. This expands affordable, youth-friendly housing choices throughout HRM, including suburban and rural communities, by increasing gentle-density options without requiring large new developments.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Affordable and Flexible Housing Initiatives: Repurpose vacant buildings, support secondary suites and co‑housing projects, and offer renovation grants or tax incentives for landlords to expand affordable, youth‑friendly housing options.

Program: Cogswell District Project – Green Stormwater Infrastructure
Description: HRM’s Cogswell District redevelopment integrates green stormwater infrastructure into new complete streets and public spaces, including bioretention planters (rain gardens), tree-lined medians, stormwater planters, and permeable surfaces. These features capture and filter runoff before it reaches Halifax Harbour, reduce localized flooding, and enhance groundwater recharge and climate resilience in a dense urban district.
Solution: Green stormwater infrastructure in towns: Install rain gardens, bioswales, permeable paving, and tree canopies in neighbourhoods to reduce flooding, recharge groundwater, and improve urban resilience.

Description: Halifax Regional Municipality operates a shared thermal loop in downtown Dartmouth that captures and redistributes recovered heat to multiple civic buildings at Alderney Landing. By using heat recovery and centralized heating/cooling for a cluster of dense municipal facilities, the project functions as a small district energy system that reduces reliance on electric resistance heating and lowers per‑unit energy costs.
Solution: District heating and shared thermal systems: Develop small-scale district heating (biomass, waste heat recovery, geo) in dense communities or industrial parks to reduce reliance on electrical heating, lower per‑unit energy costs and capture local fuel resources.

Program: Halifax Volunteer Awards and Volunteer Conference
Description: Each spring during National Volunteer Week, Halifax Regional Municipality hosts a citywide celebration that recognizes outstanding volunteers and convenes a conference with workshops, networking, and a volunteer fair-style environment for nonprofits to recruit new helpers. By pairing public recognition with practical recruitment and engagement activities, the event functions as an annual community giving and volunteer festival that energizes philanthropy and strengthens the nonprofit ecosystem.
Solution: Annual Community Giving and Volunteer Festivals: Organize yearly festivals that combine volunteer recruitment, donor drives, recognition ceremonies, and mini-grants to energize philanthropy and celebrate community contributions.

Description: Halifax Regional Municipality provides an annual property tax exemption for eligible low-income homeowners, reducing or eliminating the amount of residential property tax owed. By lowering recurring housing costs, this municipal tax-relief incentive helps young residents and new families who meet income thresholds to stabilize finances early on and build roots in the community instead of relocating.
Solution: Local Loyalty and Tax-Relief Incentives: Community-led incentive packages—such as discounts from local businesses, property-tax deferral programs run by municipalities, or rebate vouchers from chambers of commerce—help reduce early household costs for young residents committing to stay.

Program: Settlement Services – Health and Social Service Navigation
Organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
Description: ISANS settlement counsellors act as navigators for newcomers, helping them register for MSI, find a family doctor, understand specialist waitlists, and book medical and mental-health appointments. They also provide form-filling support, connect clients to language and interpretation for care, help apply for income and medication subsidies, and follow up to ensure people can attend and adhere to care plans.
Solution: Community health navigator program: Locally based navigators help residents understand waitlists, book appointments, complete forms, apply for subsidized services, and follow up—reducing missed appointments and improving continuity of care.
Address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

Program: Language Interpretation & Translation Services (LITS) and English Language Programs
Organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
Description: ISANS provides trained interpreters and translators in dozens of languages to help newcomers and service providers communicate clearly in legal, health, education, and community settings. Alongside LITS, ISANS delivers English classes and volunteer-led conversation circles that build everyday language skills and foster cross-cultural exchange—directly reducing communication barriers and strengthening inclusion.
Solution: Community Language and Interpretation Networks: Organize volunteer interpreter pools and community language classes (including Mi'kmaq language learning support) to lower communication barriers for newcomers and strengthen cross-cultural exchange.
Address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

Program: Anti-Racism and Anti-Oppression Training for Workplaces and Communities
Organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
Description: ISANS provides interactive workshops that equip employers, service providers, and community members with allyship skills and safe bystander intervention techniques to address racism and xenophobia. Training covers how to recognize microaggressions, safely step in when harm occurs, and support newcomers and racialized people who experience discrimination in neighbourhoods and workplaces.
Solution: Community Allyship and Bystander Intervention Campaigns: Run neighbourhood campaigns and short workshops that teach practical allyship behaviours, safe bystander interventions, and how to support people experiencing racism, homophobia, transphobia, or ableism.
Address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

Description: The Indigenous Justice Program at the Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre provides restorative circles, peacemaking, and mediation for urban Indigenous community members. Elders, Knowledge Keepers, and trained community volunteers facilitate talking circles that address incidents of interpersonal harm and discrimination, focusing on healing, accountability, and relationship repair rather than punishment. The program connects participants with supports and uses culturally grounded practices to re...
Solution: Neighbourhood Restorative Justice and Conflict Resolution: Set up restorative circles and mediation services facilitated by trained community volunteers to address interpersonal discrimination incidents and rebuild trust without defaulting to punitive systems.

Program: Urban Indigenous Peer Outreach and Wellness Supports
Description: The Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre provides culturally safe, trauma-informed drop-in supports where Indigenous peer workers and volunteers offer wellness check-ins, traditional cultural activities, and navigation to mental health and community services. The program centers Mi’kmaw worldviews and lived experience to reduce barriers for people facing racism, homelessness, and discrimination, and provides warm referrals to specialized care.
Solution: Community Mental Health Peer Support Network: Train peer-support volunteers from diverse backgrounds to provide culturally safe mental-health drop-in hours, referral navigation, and trauma-informed support for people facing discrimination.

Description: Ecology Action Centre works with municipalities and community organizations across Nova Scotia to design and implement solar-plus-battery systems at community buildings—such as halls and libraries—so they can serve as resilience hubs during outages. The projects reduce energy costs year-round, provide critical services to vulnerable residents when the grid is down, and build local capacity by demonstrating scalable microgrid solutions.
Solution: Resilience hubs and community backup power: Equip schools, libraries or community centres with solar + battery microgrids to serve as resilience hubs during outages, providing critical services and protecting vulnerable residents while demonstrating local reliability solutions.

Description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia’s Team Build program engages companies in structured employee volunteer days on construction sites, combining hands‑on service with safety training and team development. Businesses also provide in‑kind materials, skilled pro bono labour, and sponsorships that underwrite tools, training, and operational improvements. This integrated employer partnership model strengthens Habitat’s capacity and the broader community housing ecosystem to deliver lasting social im...
Solution: Business–Community Partnership Network: Organize a local employer network for in-kind support, payroll-giving, pro bono services, employee volunteer days, and sponsorship of capacity-building efforts for nonprofits.

Description: Volta operates a large innovation hub in downtown Halifax that offers coworking desks, private offices, high-speed internet, meeting rooms, and mail services for companies and independent professionals. Flexible memberships and shared amenities make it easier for remote workers and startups to access national and international opportunities while living locally. This directly supports wage competitiveness by connecting Nova Scotians to higher-paying remote roles and clients.
Challenge: Wage competitiveness versus rising living costs
Solution: Shared Workspaces, Broadband Hubs and Remote Work Support: Create affordable co-working spaces with high-speed internet, meeting rooms and mail services so remote workers and freelancers can access higher-paying remote jobs while living locally.
Address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

Description: Volta highlights startup founders and teams through written profiles, videos, and stage time at community events, often featuring Nova Scotians who moved away and returned to launch or scale companies in Halifax. By showcasing these returner success stories across its website and social channels, Volta promotes clear examples of how to come back and plug into the local tech and startup ecosystem.
Solution: Returner Showcases and Success Stories: Regularly highlight returning residents who have built businesses or careers locally through profiles, events and social media to normalize and promote return pathways.
Address: 1505 Barrington Street, 7th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

Program: Volta Residency (Flexible Office and Desk Space)
Description: Volta provides early-stage startups with affordable, month-to-month desk and private office rentals in downtown Halifax, lowering upfront space costs and commitment risk. This flexible leasing model directly addresses the barrier of costly spaces by offering reduced-rate, short-term arrangements in a key urban corridor, helping founders test and scale without long leases.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Municipal Low-Rent and Flexible Lease Programs: Advocate for municipal policies that offer reduced rent, rent-to-own paths, or short-term flexible leases for startups in key corridors, plus incentives for landlords who host new local businesses.
Address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

Description: Volta hosts DemoCamp and community showcase nights where founders, makers, and students give live product demos (no slides) to the public, local businesses, and investors. By convening diverse stakeholders to see and test early-stage products, these events deliver rapid feedback, create visibility, and spark early customer and partnership leads for Nova Scotia ventures.
Solution: Neighbourhood Demo Days and Marketplaces: Organize regular events where local innovators, makers, and students present prototypes and businesses to community members and small buyers, generating feedback, early sales, and local visibility.
Address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

Program: Volta Startup Open Houses & Talent Nights
Description: Volta regularly hosts Startup Open Houses, Talent Nights, and employer info sessions that bring high-growth startups together with students, recent grads, and career changers. Participating companies showcase their products, outline co-op/internship and junior roles, and meet candidates in an accessible open-house format, helping demystify career paths and highlight growth in Nova Scotia’s innovation economy.
Solution: Local Business & Career Showcases: Host regular open-house events that let local businesses, trades, and creative enterprises present career pathways, apprenticeships and internships to high-school and post-secondary students and job-seekers, making pathways and growth visible.
Address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

Description: Downtown Truro Partnership offers small, community-driven grants for murals, pop-up shows, window galleries, and other creative placemaking led by local and emerging artists. With funding sourced from the local business community and a streamlined local review, the program moves modest grants quickly to projects that build vibrancy and accessibility in Truro’s downtown.
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
Solution: Community Arts Microgrants: Small, locally administered grants (e.g., $250–$5,000) funded by municipal seed money, businesses, and citizen donations to support pop-up shows, youth projects, community murals, and emerging artists. Local review panels allocate funds quickly and provide simple reporting to lower barriers.

Description: WFM2Go aggregates, packs, and delivers products from farmers and fishers through a province-wide online marketplace with multiple rural pickup points. The platform provides cooperative marketing, e‑commerce, and shared logistics so producers can reach customers year‑round without building their own retail or distribution systems, keeping more of the value and jobs in rural communities.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Local Food and Value‑Added Processing: Support community kitchens, shared processing facilities and cooperative marketing for farmers and fishers to add value locally, increase year‑round jobs and create new exportable products.

Program: Money Matters & Housing Information Sessions (Halifax Public Libraries)
Description: Halifax Public Libraries hosts free Money Matters financial literacy workshops and periodic tenant/first-time homebuyer information sessions in partnership with community experts. These sessions provide budgeting, credit-building, and housing education that help young people plan for stable housing and navigate the rental and homebuying process at low or no cost.
Challenge: Wage competitiveness versus rising living costs
Solution: Financial Counseling, Rent-to-Own Pathways and Housing Navigation: Offer free or low-cost financial coaching, tenant/first-time-buyer workshops and community-led rent-to-own pilot programs to help young people plan and secure stable housing without excessive cost burden.
Address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

Description: Halifax Public Libraries’ ELL program hosts free conversation clubs, tutoring, and newcomer workshops in branches across the municipality, providing accessible, community-based language learning. Many sessions build everyday and workplace English, including resume and interview language, customer-service interactions, and Canadian workplace culture and customs. By connecting newcomers and youth with volunteer facilitators and peers in library community spaces, the program supports quicker int...
Solution: Community-led Language & Workplace Culture Orientation: Offer practical workplace English/French and local workplace customs courses in community centres to help internationally trained people and youth integrate quickly into local jobs.
Address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

Program: Open Libraries (Self-Service Extended Hours) – Sheet Harbour Public Library
Description: Halifax Public Libraries’ Open Libraries program extends access to the Sheet Harbour branch beyond staffed hours, letting cardholders enter the building to use high-speed Wi‑Fi, public computers, printers, and study spaces. This creates a reliable connectivity hub where residents can work remotely, take online classes, attend telehealth appointments in private rooms, and access digital government services even if they lack home internet.
Solution: Library and Community Hub Connectivity Nodes: Upgrade libraries, municipal halls, and community centres as public connectivity hubs with reliable broadband, extended hours, private work pods, and printing services so residents can access remote work, education, telehealth, and government services without needing home internet.

Description: Halifax Public Libraries offers free, bookable private rooms, Wi‑Fi, and on-site computers/headsets that residents use to join virtual medical and mental‑health appointments. Library staff provide one‑on‑one technology assistance (e.g., setting up Zoom/Teams, testing microphones/cameras) and can connect patrons with newcomer/interpretation supports available through partner services, effectively operating as community telehealth hubs.
Solution: Local telehealth hubs: Libraries, community centres, or co-working spaces host private, Wi‑Fi‑equipped booths where residents can join virtual appointments, with staff available to assist with technology and interpretation.
Address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

Program: Newcomer Services and English Conversation Groups (Central Library)
Description: Halifax Central Library serves as a community-led newcomer hub, hosting volunteer-run English Conversation Groups, newcomer social meetups, and information sessions that help with everyday paperwork and system navigation. Staff and partners offer resume and job-search workshops and connect participants with cultural mentors and local donation networks (including periodic winter-gear and household starter drives) to reduce barriers to settling in.
Solution: Peer-led Newcomer Settlement Hubs: Establish volunteer-run hubs where newcomers can get help with paperwork, language-conversation groups, job-search coaching, connections to cultural mentors, and access to donated household items to ease settlement.
Address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

Program: Library of Things: Musical Instruments & Recording Kits
Description: Halifax Public Libraries lends instruments (e.g., guitars, ukuleles) and portable recording gear, and provides in-branch studios for audio production. This equipment access model functions as an arts-focused lending library, reducing financial barriers for emerging artists and youth to create music, podcasts, and performance-ready material.
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
Solution: Timebanking and Equipment Libraries: Create a community timebank where volunteers trade skills (e.g., event planning for rehearsal time) and a tool/equipment library where sound, lighting, and art supplies can be borrowed, lowering barriers for small-scale productions.
Address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

Description: Chebucto Connections offers free small-group English classes and conversation circles at its community hub in Spryfield, making language learning accessible where people live. Sessions focus on everyday and workplace English, communication styles, scheduling, safety, and rights at work, and often connect participants to local employers and services. This community-led approach helps internationally trained residents and youth quickly gain the language and cultural fluency needed to secure and...
Solution: Community-led Language & Workplace Culture Orientation: Offer practical workplace English/French and local workplace customs courses in community centres to help internationally trained people and youth integrate quickly into local jobs.
Address: 531 Herring Cove Road, Suite 200, Halifax, NS B3R 1X3

Description: United Way Halifax offers small, community-funded grants to residents and grassroots groups to run local projects that build belonging, services, and social enterprises. For young people returning to the region, these micro-grants can offset immediate costs of launching community initiatives or pilot programs, creating welcoming on-ramps to re-engage and put down roots.
Solution: Returner Microgrant Program: Establish community-funded microgrants to help young people cover relocation costs, short-term housing, or startup expenses when returning to the area, administered by a local nonprofit or chamber of commerce.
Address: 46 Portland Street, 7th Floor, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1H4

Program: Workplace Campaigns and Day of Caring
Description: United Way Halifax convenes local employers to run Workplace Campaigns that enable payroll giving and corporate donations, channeling sustained funding to frontline nonprofits. Through Day of Caring, they organize employer-led volunteer days to complete hands‑on projects for community agencies, and they broker in‑kind and pro bono support from business partners. Corporate sponsorships also help fund community capacity‑building initiatives, training, and grants that strengthen nonprofit operat...
Solution: Business–Community Partnership Network: Organize a local employer network for in-kind support, payroll-giving, pro bono services, employee volunteer days, and sponsorship of capacity-building efforts for nonprofits.

Description: United Way Halifax activates the global Giving Tuesday movement locally through online crowdfunding appeals that spotlight resident and neighborhood stories tied to priority community programs. Campaigns often feature limited-time matching gifts or challenge grants from local companies, encouraging small donations that are multiplied to support underfunded social services in HRM.
Solution: Local Crowdfunding and Storytelling Campaigns: Run community crowdfunding drives that pair personal stories with small matching gifts from local businesses to mobilize resident giving and spotlight underfunded programs.

Program: Agency Learning and Capacity Building Sessions
Description: United Way Halifax convenes regular learning sessions for partner and funded agencies on fundraising strategy, donor stewardship, board governance, program evaluation, and volunteer management. Workshops feature local professionals—such as accountants, fundraisers, and retired nonprofit executives—who facilitate training and provide mentorship, helping organizations strengthen systems and sustain community impact.
Solution: Capacity-Building Workshops and Mentorship: Host regular training series (fundraising, governance, impact measurement, volunteer management) led by local professionals and retired leaders to strengthen nonprofit skillsets.

Description: The Town of Wolfville’s Community Partnership Program provides predictable, often multi‑year operating funding agreements and in‑kind supports (such as approved fee waivers for municipal facility use) to key community organizations. This implements the solution by creating formal municipal partnership agreements and stabilizing core funding for local arts, culture, recreation, and social supports that strengthen community life for young people.
Solution: Local Policy and Municipal Partnership Advocacy: Coordinate resident and nonprofit advocacy for municipal policies that provide stable operating grants, fee waivers for community spaces, and partnership agreements that recognize the value of local social infrastructure.

Description: Wolfville’s low-income property tax exemption provides an annual reduction in residential property taxes for eligible property owners. By lowering essential housing expenses, the program functions as a local tax-relief incentive that helps younger residents and families meet early household costs and encourages them to remain in the community.
Solution: Local Loyalty and Tax-Relief Incentives: Community-led incentive packages—such as discounts from local businesses, property-tax deferral programs run by municipalities, or rebate vouchers from chambers of commerce—help reduce early household costs for young residents committing to stay.

Description: White Point packages accommodations with hands-on workshops, artist talks, live music, and culinary experiences led by Nova Scotian creators throughout the year. These bookable cultural weekends are promoted to regional visitors and engage local artisans, musicians, and producers as paid facilitators. The model directly supports creatives and nearby small businesses while offering immersive local culture to guests.
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
Solution: Cultural Tourism and Local Experience Packages: Develop walking tours, seasonal cultural weekends, and artist studio visits marketed regionally. Small businesses, B&Bs, and creatives collaborate to create packages that generate revenue and profile for local culture.
Address: 75 White Point Beach Resort Road, White Point, NS B0T 1G0

Organization: Health Services Foundation of the South Shore
Description: The Health Services Foundation of the South Shore funds tuition and professional education for health workers serving South Shore Regional Hospital and Fishermen’s Memorial Hospital, typically linked to return‑of‑service commitments. These grants are coordinated with Nova Scotia Health employer supports so that foundation contributions match or top up employer tuition‑reimbursement, easing student loan burdens and anchoring talent locally.
Solution: Employer–Community Tuition Repayment Network: A coalition where local employers offer partial tuition-repayment or loan-assistance packages for staff, with community foundations or municipalities providing matching contributions to amplify impact.
Address: 90 Glen Allan Drive, Bridgewater, NS B4V 3S6

Program: Adsum Affordable & Supportive Housing (including Sunflower Court)
Description: Adsum for Women & Children develops and stewards permanently affordable and supportive housing—such as Sunflower Court—by acquiring and holding land and buildings under nonprofit, community-based governance. This model keeps housing off the speculative market and ensures long-term affordability for women, gender-diverse people, and families, directly addressing rising housing costs with a community-controlled approach consistent with community land trust principles.
Challenge: Wage competitiveness versus rising living costs
Solution: Community Land Trusts for Affordable Housing: Create or expand locally governed community land trusts that buy and hold land for permanently affordable rental and ownership housing, prioritizing young workers and families and stabilizing long-term housing costs.

Description: Dalhousie University’s Career & Co-op runs myCareer, a matching platform that connects students and alumni with Nova Scotia employers. Employers post full-time, part-time, co-op, internship, contract, and project-based roles while alumni create profiles showcasing skills for targeted outreach. The team also tracks graduate outcomes and location preferences through surveys, informing strategies to engage alumni who intend to return and easing re-entry with short-term opportunities.
Solution: Alumni-to-Employer Matching Platform: Build a lightweight local platform to match alumni skills with employer needs, track return intentions, and advertise short-term project or contract work to ease re-entry.

Program: Office of Commercialization and Industry Engagement (OCIE)
Description: Dalhousie’s OCIE provides researchers and spinout teams with shared commercialization services such as IP assessment, patenting and licensing support, standard research and collaboration agreements, and startup formation guidance. By centralizing templates, legal/IP clinics, and industry matchmaking, OCIE reduces friction and cost in translating research into Nova Scotia-based companies.
Solution: Shared Commercialization Services: Form cooperative services (legal templates, IP clinics, accounting, marketing) available at low cost to startups and researchers, lowering the barrier to spin out local ventures.

Description: Dalhousie’s Student Ambassadors are trained hosts who lead guided campus and neighbourhood tours for prospective students and their families, sharing personal experiences and practical insights about life in Halifax. By offering authentic peer-to-peer hospitality and introductions to campus services and local amenities, they help young people see Nova Scotia as a vibrant place to study, work, and build a future.
Solution: Neighbourhood Hospitality & Host Programs: Train volunteers from across the community to serve as 'hosts' for visiting journalists, prospective investors, students and job candidates—offering authentic local tours, introductions and hospitality that change perceptions.

Program: NSCECE Career Services and Employer Partnerships
Organization: Nova Scotia College of Early Childhood Education (NSCECE)
Description: The Nova Scotia College of Early Childhood Education leads community-facing recruitment drives—info sessions, job fairs, and a province-wide job board—that promote clear career pathways in childcare from entry roles to Level 3 ECEs. Through employer partnerships with licensed centres across the province, NSCECE helps operators advertise roles (including hiring incentives like signing bonuses or enhanced starting wages where offered) and matches local candidates to vacancies, improving retenti...
Solution: Local Recruitment Campaigns and Wage Supplements: Community coalitions run recruitment drives highlighting local career ladders in childcare, offering small wage supplements or signing bonuses funded by local businesses and foundations to retain staff.

Description: TnGo operates fixed routes alongside app/phone‑bookable on-demand service areas that use dynamic scheduling to cover lower‑density neighborhoods cost‑effectively. This approach prototypes and deploys microtransit scheduling tools locally, mirroring the solution’s emphasis on low‑cost mobility innovation that improves access to work, education, and services in a small‑city/rural context.
Solution: Local Mobility Innovation Challenges: Host hackathons or challenge grants inviting students, entrepreneurs and civic groups to prototype low-cost mobility solutions—apps for ride-matching, scheduling tools for microtransit, or cargo-bike delivery pilots—then incubate promising ideas locally.

Description: The Town of Truro’s Planning & Development and Building Inspection Office provides walk-in support to residents and contractors for permit applications. Staff assist with completing forms, identifying required drawings and approvals, and explaining fees and timelines, helping ensure submissions are complete and reducing re-submission rates.
Solution: Community Permit Navigation Hubs: Set up volunteer-run or municipally partnered hubs where residents and small developers receive in-person help filling applications, understanding fees, and preparing supporting documents to reduce mistakes and re-submissions.

Description: The Town of Truro has undertaken a voluntary buyout and relocation program for properties repeatedly impacted by flooding along the Salmon River and McClures Brook floodplains. The program identifies high-risk parcels through flood-risk mapping, offers fair-market compensation and relocation assistance to willing homeowners, and converts acquired lands to open space and flood storage areas, creating green buffers that reduce future risk.
Solution: Managed retreat planning and land-swap initiatives: Community-driven planning that identifies high-risk parcels, offers fair relocation incentives or land-swaps, and converts vulnerable sites to open space or coastal buffers.

Organization: Home of the Guardian Angel (Chebucto Family Centre)
Description: The Chebucto Family Centre’s Bulk Food Buying Club pools participants’ funds to purchase staple foods and produce at wholesale prices, with shares divided by volunteers for pickup. The centre also hosts community kitchen sessions and family cooking programs, directly lowering grocery costs and building cooking confidence for young families and low-wage households.
Challenge: Wage competitiveness versus rising living costs
Solution: Food Co-ops, Bulk Buying and Community Kitchens: Develop community-run food cooperatives, bulk-buy programs and shared cooking facilities to lower household grocery costs and build food security for young families and low-wage workers.

Description: Nova Scotia Health facilitates structured job-shadow (observership) experiences that allow students and jobseekers to spend short periods following clinicians, administrators, and technical staff across hospital departments. These observational placements, which can span multiple days, expose participants to mid- and senior-level roles and help them build professional networks, directly reducing barriers to advancement in health careers.
Challenge: Thin job density and limited career ladders
Solution: Job Shadowing Weeks and Rotational Placements: Organize community-wide job-shadow and short rotational placement weeks where young people experience mid- and senior-level roles across employers, building networks and reducing barriers to advancement.

Description: Nova Scotia Health coordinates clinical placements for nursing, medicine, and allied health students across hospitals and community sites in all zones of the province. Working directly with Nova Scotia universities/colleges and local preceptors, the program organizes placements, onsite mentorship, and transition‑to‑practice connections that support recruitment and long‑term retention of new graduates in the communities where they train.
Solution: Healthcare student placement and retention partnerships: Community groups collaborate with regional colleges and universities to host clinical placements, offer homestays, and create mentorship and incentive packages that encourage new graduates to stay or return.

Description: Nova Scotia Health’s PFPA program engages volunteer advisors in shaping health services and policy across the province. To remove financial barriers, the program reimburses volunteers for practical costs such as mileage, parking, transit fares, and, when needed, childcare so caregivers and younger adults can participate in meetings, committees, and co-design sessions.
Solution: Childcare and Transportation Stipends for Volunteers: Offer small stipends or vouchers to cover childcare, transit, or parking for volunteers—especially younger people and caregivers—to remove practical barriers to participation.
Address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

Program: People’s Place: Antigonish Town & County Library
Description: People’s Place operates as a community hub with robust broadband, free public Wi‑Fi and computers, printing/scanning, and multiple bookable meeting and study rooms for quiet, private use. Evening and weekend hours, along with staffed support, enable residents to do remote work, complete online education, hold telehealth appointments, and access digital government services without needing home internet.
Solution: Library and Community Hub Connectivity Nodes: Upgrade libraries, municipal halls, and community centres as public connectivity hubs with reliable broadband, extended hours, private work pods, and printing services so residents can access remote work, education, telehealth, and government services without needing home internet.

Program: Meeting Rooms and Public Computer Access
Description: Cape Breton Regional Library’s McConnell Library branch offers free, bookable study/meeting rooms, reliable Wi‑Fi, and public computers with webcams/headsets that patrons use for virtual doctor and counselling visits. Library staff provide basic tech help to get connected and maintain a quiet, private environment—functioning as a local telehealth access point for residents without suitable home internet or space.
Solution: Local telehealth hubs: Libraries, community centres, or co-working spaces host private, Wi‑Fi‑equipped booths where residents can join virtual appointments, with staff available to assist with technology and interpretation.

Description: A community makerspace featuring 3D printing, laser cutting, sewing machines, electronics, and multimedia tools, housed in the library at the Lunenburg County Lifestyle Centre. Through workshops, drop-in access, and staff guidance, it helps youth and newcomers build technical competencies, create prototypes and portfolios, and explore entrepreneurship or trades pathways using shared equipment.
Solution: Shared Maker Spaces and Tool Libraries: Establish or expand community maker spaces and tool libraries that allow young people and newcomers to practise trade and tech skills, build portfolios and access equipment for training or small business starts.
Address: 135 North Park Street, Bridgewater, NS B4V 9B3

Program: Nova Scotia Health Recruitment – Relocation Assistance and Signing Bonuses
Description: Nova Scotia Health provides relocation allowances and signing bonuses to qualified candidates who accept positions across the province, including Nova Scotians returning after completing education or training out of province. These funds function as welcome grants that can be applied to moving expenses, short-term housing deposits, and other start-up costs of resettling in a Nova Scotia community.
Solution: Return-to-Community Welcome Grants: Small cash grants or relocation bonuses funded by municipalities, community foundations and local businesses for people who return to Nova Scotia after completing education elsewhere, used for housing deposits, moving costs or startup expenses.
Address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

Program: The North Grove Early Years Programs (Free and Pay-What-You-Can)
Description: The North Grove offers free early learning and child development programs, along with no-cost on-site childminding that enables parents to attend skills training, appointments, or employment supports. Programs operate at no fee or pay-what-you-can and are sustained by a blend of public funding, donations, and local fundraising—directly embodying flexible, transparent fee practices to reduce childcare barriers.
Solution: Flexible Fee Models and Sliding-scale Policies: Community-run centres adopt transparent sliding-scale fee structures, sibling discounts and pay-what-you-can days, supported by local fundraising to sustain operations while increasing affordability.

Program: Peer Outreach and Community Drop-in Mental Health Supports
Description: The Ally Centre of Cape Breton operates a low-barrier drop-in where peer workers and volunteers with lived experience provide trauma-informed mental health support, harm reduction, and navigation to housing, addictions, and clinical services. The program prioritizes culturally safe care for people who face discrimination, including Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, and 2SLGBTQ+ community members, and makes warm referrals to local health providers.
Solution: Community Mental Health Peer Support Network: Train peer-support volunteers from diverse backgrounds to provide culturally safe mental-health drop-in hours, referral navigation, and trauma-informed support for people facing discrimination.

Program: Town of Bridgewater Sustainable Procurement Policy
Description: The Town of Bridgewater’s procurement framework integrates social and economic value, asking suppliers to demonstrate local workforce development approaches—such as employing Nova Scotia apprentices, creating co-op or internship placements, and committing to training and advancement—especially in infrastructure and clean energy projects. This policy uses municipal purchasing power to cultivate stable, quality roles and clearer advancement pathways for local residents.
Challenge: Thin job density and limited career ladders
Solution: Municipal Procurement for Local Career Development: Adopt municipal procurement clauses that prioritize local suppliers who commit to local hiring, apprenticeships or career-ladder guarantees, using public spend to grow quality roles.

Program: Energize Bridgewater (Clean Energy Financing and Community Projects)
Description: Energize Bridgewater helps residents and local businesses adopt rooftop solar and other clean energy upgrades through a PACE-style financing program and community partnerships, creating steady work for local installers and trades. The initiative lowers energy costs for participants and uses a revolving fund approach so repayments and municipal energy savings can be directed into further clean-energy projects and community services that benefit the town.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Community Energy and Climate Projects: Develop small‑scale renewable projects (solar co‑ops, biomass) that create local jobs, lower energy costs and generate revenue that can be reinvested in community services.

Program: Low Income Property Tax Exemption Program
Description: The Town of Bridgewater offers a low-income property tax exemption that reduces annual property tax bills for qualifying households. This tax-relief incentive eases early housing costs—especially helpful for younger homeowners and families—making it more affordable to stay in Bridgewater and invest in local life and careers.
Solution: Local Loyalty and Tax-Relief Incentives: Community-led incentive packages—such as discounts from local businesses, property-tax deferral programs run by municipalities, or rebate vouchers from chambers of commerce—help reduce early household costs for young residents committing to stay.

Program: Community Grant Program (Facility Infrastructure & Safety Upgrades)
Description: The Municipality of East Hants provides capital grants and staff advisory support to help community halls, churches and non-profits complete minor renovations and safety upgrades needed for licensed child care (e.g., exits, accessibility, washrooms, fire safety). This funding and guidance lowers start-up costs and accelerates the conversion of shared community spaces into licensed child care capacity.
Solution: Shared Space Licensing Support Program: A community-led service assists churches, schools and community halls with licensing, minor renovations and health/safety compliance so they can more quickly and affordably open licensed childcare capacity.

Program: Kings County Regional Emergency Management Organization (REMO)
Organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
Description: Kings REMO coordinates municipal emergency preparedness, training, and volunteer engagement across communities in Kings County. The program helps organize and equip community comfort centres and volunteer teams for evacuation support, sandbagging, and local communications during floods and storms, and integrates these volunteers with municipal services and partner agencies like the Red Cross. Ongoing exercises and public education build neighborhood-level capacity to respond and recover quickly.
Solution: Community emergency preparedness teams: Train and equip local volunteer response teams for evacuation coordination, sandbagging, temporary shelters, and communications during storms and floods.
Address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

Organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
Description: The Municipality of the District of Lunenburg advanced rural connectivity by setting aside local funds and collaborating with volunteers and industry partners to prepare applications to provincial and federal broadband programs. By providing municipal match funding and coordinating partner contributions, the initiative leveraged larger grants and ISP co‑investment to expand reliable high‑speed service across underserved communities.
Solution: Community Mobility Fundraising and Grant Support: Create a local fund and a volunteer grant-writing team to support transit and broadband projects. Pool donations, apply for government infrastructure programs, and provide match funding to unlock larger grants.

Organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
Description: MODL’s program enables residents to install rooftop solar PV, solar hot water, and other upgrades with structured support. The municipality assists with permit requirements, provides template documents and pre-approved work scopes, and coordinates with building/electrical inspectors and Nova Scotia Power to streamline and fast‑track approvals, cutting administrative time and costs to speed distributed energy deployment.
Solution: Local permitting assistance and fast‑track for distributed energy: Municipal teams offer step‑by‑step permitting help, standard permit packages and fast‑track approvals for rooftop solar, batteries and small generation to reduce soft costs and speed deployment.

Description: This modern rural library hub provides free high-speed Wi‑Fi, public computers, and printing/scan/fax services, along with bookable study spaces for privacy during remote work or telehealth sessions. By offering dependable connectivity and on-site support, it enables residents to participate in online education, employment, healthcare, and government services despite patchy home broadband.
Solution: Library and Community Hub Connectivity Nodes: Upgrade libraries, municipal halls, and community centres as public connectivity hubs with reliable broadband, extended hours, private work pods, and printing services so residents can access remote work, education, telehealth, and government services without needing home internet.

Program: Advanced Standing (Portfolio Review) for Studio and Design Courses
Description: NSCAD University recognizes substantial prior studio practice and community-based creative work by granting advanced standing or transfer credit through formal portfolio review. Applicants submit portfolios and documentation of practice that assess equivalency to course learning outcomes, enabling them to receive credit toward certificates or progress more quickly in degree programs.
Solution: Local Credit-for-Experience Programs: Partner with regional colleges to create formal processes where verified community work experience, portfolios or employer references convert to course credit or advanced standing toward certificates.

Description: NSCAD’s recurring Student Art Sale is a public marketplace where students present and sell new work—including design objects, functional prototypes, and creative products—directly to community members and local retailers. The event provides immediate user feedback, early revenue, and commissioning opportunities, helping emerging creatives validate offerings and connect with local buyers.
Solution: Neighbourhood Demo Days and Marketplaces: Organize regular events where local innovators, makers, and students present prototypes and businesses to community members and small buyers, generating feedback, early sales, and local visibility.

Description: MentorAbility NS, coordinated locally by TEAM Work Cooperative, arranges short-term career mentorships that connect youth and adults with disabilities to employers and professionals in sectors like skilled trades, IT, hospitality, and the arts. Participants explore occupations through job shadowing and guided networking, building confidence, inclusive connections, and clearer pathways to work and apprenticeships in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Community Mentorship Circles for Youth: Create mentorship programs pairing youth from marginalized groups with local professionals, tradespeople, and artists to build networks, career pathways, apprenticeships, and confidence to stay or return home.

Program: Nursing Community Assessment Service (NCAS) – Nova Scotia Pathway
Description: Through NSCN, internationally educated nurses complete NCAS multi-method competency assessments (computer-based testing, simulation, and OSCE-style stations) at local test sites to validate readiness for practice in Nova Scotia. The results produce an evidence-based report that informs licensing and targeted bridging, effectively certifying practical competencies aligned with employer and health-system needs to speed workforce entry.
