Solution: On-site Childcare Pilot Grants for Small Businesses: Municipalities offer small grants and technical support for small businesses and co-working spaces to pilot on-site childcare pods, demonstrating feasibility and encouraging wider adoption.
Address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

Description: New Ross Family Resource Centre delivers drop-in playgroups, peer mentoring, and parenting workshops led by ECE professionals, with support from community volunteers and experienced parents. The centre offers short-term child-minding during programs and appointments, creating relief care that helps parents manage stress and maintain employment or pursue training opportunities.
Solution: Volunteer Mentor Networks for New Parents: Experienced parents and local ECE professionals volunteer through community programs to provide drop-in support, parenting workshops and short-term relief care to reduce stress and allow workforce participation.

Program: YMCA Child Care – Community Partnerships & New Site Development
Description: YMCA of Greater Halifax/Dartmouth partners with schools, churches and community halls to open licensed child care in shared spaces. The YMCA team manages the provincial licensing process, coordinates minor renovations (e.g., washrooms, secure access, fire safety) and implements health and safety protocols so new spaces can come online faster and at lower cost.
Solution: Shared Space Licensing Support Program: A community-led service assists churches, schools and community halls with licensing, minor renovations and health/safety compliance so they can more quickly and affordably open licensed childcare capacity.

Program: YMCA Child Care – Community Site Development
Description: YMCA of Cape Breton collaborates with schools, parishes and community organizations to establish licensed child care programs in existing community facilities. The YMCA team navigates licensing requirements, oversees minor renovations for code and health/safety compliance, and provides staff training and operating systems to bring new spaces online efficiently.
Solution: Shared Space Licensing Support Program: A community-led service assists churches, schools and community halls with licensing, minor renovations and health/safety compliance so they can more quickly and affordably open licensed childcare capacity.

Description: The CIIF, administered by the Nova Scotia Co-operative Council with Atlantic credit unions, aggregates funds from local individuals and institutions to provide patient, early-stage capital to small and growing businesses and social enterprises across Nova Scotia. Beyond financing, CIIF leverages a network of retired entrepreneurs, industry professionals, and credit union advisors to mentor founders, mirroring an angel co-op that pairs pooled community capital with hands-on guidance.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Local Angel Co-op Network: Form a cooperative of local high-net-worth individuals, retired entrepreneurs, and professionals who pool capital and expertise to make small early-stage investments and mentor founders in the community.
Address: 111 Ilsley Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1S8

Description: A province-wide financing program administered through credit unions to support small businesses and co-operatives, including social enterprises. By improving access to capital and providing advisory support, it enables community-serving organizations to start or scale revenue-generating operations, formalize hiring (often of young workers), and reduce reliance on grants. This strengthens sustainable funding for social programs through predictable earned income.
Solution: Social Enterprise Incubator: Support local social enterprises that generate earned revenue to hire staff for community services, creating jobs for young people and sustainable funding for social programs.

Program: CUA Microloan and Credit-Builder Solutions for Entrepreneurs
Description: As a Halifax-based credit union, CUA offers microloans and credit-building products that support startups and sole proprietors with flexible underwriting and community-focused lending. CUA also participates in the province’s credit union–delivered Small Business Loan Guarantee Program, enabling low-interest financing and credit development for diverse and early-stage entrepreneurs.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Community Loan Fund via Credit Unions: Partner with regional credit unions to create a community loan fund offering low-interest, flexible loans, microfinance, and credit-building tools targeted at startups, sole proprietors, and underrepresented entrepreneurs.

Organization: Norman Newman Centre for Entrepreneurship, Dalhousie University
Description: Launch Dal’s Ready2Launch accelerator culminates in a public Demo Day where student and research-based startups pitch to investors, industry partners, and the broader community. The event showcases prototypes and go-to-market plans, creating a forum for immediate feedback, introductions to local service providers, and early customer engagement and sales traction.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Regular Pitch Nights and Demo Days: Host monthly or quarterly community pitch events where founders present to local investors, customers, and service providers; combine with 'buy local' showcases to generate feedback, visibility, and immediate sales opportunities.

Description: The Lunenburg Makery provides a community studio with shared equipment such as sewing machines, textile tools, and workspace for craft and design projects. Entrepreneurs and makers can access the space through workshops, drop‑in sessions, and memberships, reducing the need to invest in their own equipment. This shared, pay‑as‑you‑go model supports small creative businesses and product prototyping in a low‑cost environment.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Community Equipment and Maker Spaces: Establish co-op maker spaces and equipment libraries where entrepreneurs can access tools, fabrication equipment, film/editing suites, and rehearsal space on a pay-per-use or membership basis to lower capital costs.

Program: Credit Union Small Business Loan Guarantee Program (Nova Scotia)
Organization: CUA (Credit Union Atlantic) – participating Nova Scotia credit union
Description: This program provides loans to startups and small businesses through participating Nova Scotia credit unions, backed by a government guarantee that covers a substantial portion of the lender’s risk. By sharing risk with lenders, it enables approval of loans that might otherwise be declined, improving access to capital for promising local entrepreneurs and early-stage ventures.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Small Business Guarantee Pool: Set up a risk-sharing guarantee backed by municipal or philanthropic funds to provide partial guarantees for bank loans to promising local startups, lowering lender risk and improving borrowing access.

Organization: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
Description: CSBFP is a federal loan guarantee that shares risk with banks and credit unions across Nova Scotia by guaranteeing a significant portion of eligible small business loans. This reduces lenders’ exposure and encourages financing for startups and growing firms to acquire equipment, make leasehold improvements, and fund expansion—directly addressing risk-averse lending barriers.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Small Business Guarantee Pool: Set up a risk-sharing guarantee backed by municipal or philanthropic funds to provide partial guarantees for bank loans to promising local startups, lowering lender risk and improving borrowing access.

Description: This sector-specific guarantee shares risk with financial institutions on loans to eligible farmers for breeding livestock purchases and related needs. By backing a portion of the loan, the program lowers lender risk and improves credit access for agricultural entrepreneurs, enabling growth of small farm businesses across Nova Scotia.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Small Business Guarantee Pool: Set up a risk-sharing guarantee backed by municipal or philanthropic funds to provide partial guarantees for bank loans to promising local startups, lowering lender risk and improving borrowing access.
Address: 7 Atlantic Central Drive, East Mountain, NS B6L 2Z2

Description: EDC’s EGP provides a partial guarantee to a company’s financial institution, enabling increased working capital and term lending for export-ready SMEs in Nova Scotia. By sharing the credit risk with banks, the program unlocks capital for growth, market entry, and scaling, aligning with the risk-sharing guarantee model to support entrepreneurial expansion.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Small Business Guarantee Pool: Set up a risk-sharing guarantee backed by municipal or philanthropic funds to provide partial guarantees for bank loans to promising local startups, lowering lender risk and improving borrowing access.

Program: Procurement Assistance Canada – Atlantic Region (Supplier Outreach)
Organization: Public Services and Procurement Canada (Procurement Assistance Canada – Atlantic Region)
Description: Procurement Assistance Canada (Atlantic) provides free seminars, one-on-one advisory, and meet-the-buyer events in Nova Scotia to help startups and small businesses register on CanadaBuys, find opportunities, and prepare competitive bids. By building procurement-readiness and brokering connections to federal buyers located in the province, it channels public purchasing toward local SMEs.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Community Procurement and 'Buy Local' Pledges: Mobilize institutions, non-profits, and residents to commit to buying from local startups and small businesses; coordinate procurement opportunities and procurement-ready training for local suppliers.

Program: BBI Supplier Diversity & Procurement Readiness Program
Description: BBI offers workshops and coaching on procurement processes, bid preparation, and supplier diversity certifications (e.g., CAMSC/CCAB) to help Black-owned startups and SMEs in Nova Scotia become procurement-ready. It convenes meet-the-buyer sessions with public institutions and corporate purchasers, encouraging anchors to include local Black-owned businesses in supply chains and facilitating direct connections to contracting opportunities.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Community Procurement and 'Buy Local' Pledges: Mobilize institutions, non-profits, and residents to commit to buying from local startups and small businesses; coordinate procurement opportunities and procurement-ready training for local suppliers.

Program: CWB Procurement Readiness and Supplier Diversity Program
Organization: Centre for Women in Business at Mount Saint Vincent University
Description: The Centre for Women in Business equips women-owned firms with procurement training on selling to government and large organizations, RFP response support, and introductions to supplier diversity programs (e.g., WEConnect/WBE Canada). It organizes matchmaking and buyer roundtables in Nova Scotia that encourage institutions to source from local women-led startups and SMEs, aligning purchasing with buy-local objectives.
Challenge: Barriers to entrepreneurship and access to capital
Solution: Community Procurement and 'Buy Local' Pledges: Mobilize institutions, non-profits, and residents to commit to buying from local startups and small businesses; coordinate procurement opportunities and procurement-ready training for local suppliers.

Description: The Municipality of East Hants provides an in-person permits and inspections counter where staff guide homeowners and small developers through development, building, and occupancy permit applications. Staff review checklists, confirm zoning requirements, and help assemble supporting documents and fee payments to minimize mistakes and processing delays.
Solution: Community Permit Navigation Hubs: Set up volunteer-run or municipally partnered hubs where residents and small developers receive in-person help filling applications, understanding fees, and preparing supporting documents to reduce mistakes and re-submissions.

Organization: Town of Truro; Municipality of the County of Colchester; Millbrook First Nation
Description: The Town of Truro, Municipality of Colchester, and Millbrook First Nation signed a Municipal Friendship Accord and formed a joint advisory body to put reconciliation into practice. The group, jointly led by Millbrook representatives and municipal officials, guides land-acknowledgement use across civic functions, co-develops cultural education and community events, and collaborates on planning decisions for parks and other public spaces.
Solution: Community-led Reconciliation Councils with Mi'kmaq Nations: Form local reconciliation councils co-chaired by Mi'kmaq elders and community members to guide land-acknowledgement practices, cultural education, co-developed events, and shared decision-making on community planning and public spaces.

Organization: Paqtnkek Mi’kmaw Nation; Town of Antigonish; Municipality of the County of Antigonish
Description: Paqtnkek Mi’kmaw Nation, the Town of Antigonish, and the Municipality of the County of Antigonish maintain a Friendship Accord with a joint implementation committee that brings Elders and community leaders together with municipal councillors. The committee steers respectful land-acknowledgement practices, co-develops public programs and events, and supports shared decision-making on community planning and public spaces to build an inclusive region.
Solution: Community-led Reconciliation Councils with Mi'kmaq Nations: Form local reconciliation councils co-chaired by Mi'kmaq elders and community members to guide land-acknowledgement practices, cultural education, co-developed events, and shared decision-making on community planning and public spaces.

Organization: Parks Canada in partnership with the Mi’kmaq of Nova Scotia
Description: Parks Canada collaborates with the Mi’kmaq of Nova Scotia through cooperative management and an advisory circle at Kejimkujik National Park and National Historic Site. Mi’kmaq Elders and community representatives help shape land-acknowledgement protocols, co-develop interpretive programs and cultural events, and share in decisions about trails, place names, and the design and use of public spaces in the park.
Solution: Community-led Reconciliation Councils with Mi'kmaq Nations: Form local reconciliation councils co-chaired by Mi'kmaq elders and community members to guide land-acknowledgement practices, cultural education, co-developed events, and shared decision-making on community planning and public spaces.
Address: 3005 Kejimkujik Main Parkway, Maitland Bridge, NS B0T 1B0

Description: A museum and interpretive site that documents and preserves the stories of Black Loyalists through exhibitions, guided tours, oral histories, and a heritage campus in historic Birchtown. In addition to heritage preservation, the Centre stimulates local African Nova Scotian entrepreneurship by partnering with artisans and small businesses (gift shop consignment, cultural markets) and by hosting community learning events that build heritage tourism and microenterprise skills.
Solution: African Nova Scotian Heritage and Economic Development Program: Support neighbourhood-based initiatives that preserve history (oral histories, monuments, heritage trails) while funding small-business support, entrepreneurship workshops, and mentorship targeted to African Nova Scotian residents.
Address: 119 Old Birchtown Road, Shelburne, NS B0T 1W0

Organization: Department of Communities, Culture, Tourism and Heritage (Government of Nova Scotia)
Description: The Community ACCESS-Ability Program provides cost-shared grants to municipalities and non-profit organizations to remove barriers in community facilities. Funding supports priority upgrades such as ramps, automatic doors, accessible washrooms, tactile/wayfinding signage, and assistive listening systems, often identified through community accessibility audits conducted by municipal Accessibility Advisory Committees and local volunteers. This pairs community-led assessments with micro-grant ca...
Solution: Community Accessibility Audits and Micro-Grants: Train local volunteers to run accessibility audits for public buildings and small businesses, and provide community micro-grants to implement priority accessibility upgrades (ramps, signage, hearing loops).

Program: Accessibility Directorate Grants (Capacity Building for Accessible Communities)
Organization: Accessibility Directorate, Department of Justice (Government of Nova Scotia)
Description: The Accessibility Directorate provides grants to public sector bodies (e.g., municipalities, libraries, post-secondary institutions) to build capacity to meet Nova Scotia’s Accessibility Act. Funding is commonly used to train staff and community volunteers to conduct accessibility audits, complete barrier assessments of buildings and services, and create prioritized implementation plans that lead to small, high-impact upgrades. This directly supports the solution’s audit-and-train approach an...
Solution: Community Accessibility Audits and Micro-Grants: Train local volunteers to run accessibility audits for public buildings and small businesses, and provide community micro-grants to implement priority accessibility upgrades (ramps, signage, hearing loops).

Organization: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
Description: The 50–30 Challenge is a national pledge program that invites Nova Scotia businesses and non-profits to publicly commit to achieving gender parity and greater representation of underrepresented groups in leadership. Participants receive free tools and guidance to adopt inclusive hiring and promotion practices, reduce biased requirements, and embed accessibility considerations across HR policies. Signatory organizations are listed publicly, making their commitment visible to employees, applica...
Solution: Inclusive Hiring Pledges for Local Employers: Create a community-backed pledge program that helps small and medium employers adopt inclusive hiring practices, remove biased job requirements, embed accessibility accommodations, and display a public commitment to equity.

Program: South Shore Sexual Health Centre Drop-In
Description: This sex-positive, 2SLGBTQ+-affirming centre provides confidential drop-in support, education, and safer-sex supplies for youth and adults. Staff offer peer support and navigation, make referrals to mental-health and primary care providers, and keep resource lists for emergency shelter and housing supports across the South Shore.
Solution: 2SLGBTQ+ Safe Spaces and Drop-in Centres: Fund and volunteer for community drop-in centres that provide peer support, mental-health referrals, sex-positive education, and emergency housing lists for 2SLGBTQ+ youth and adults facing discrimination or family rejection.

Description: Autism Nova Scotia’s employment programs, including EmploymentWorks, pair autistic youth and young adults with workplace mentors and local employers for skill-building, job sampling, and networking. These mentorship experiences help participants identify strengths, navigate career pathways, and transition into Nova Scotia’s workforce with the supports and community connections needed to thrive.
Solution: Community Mentorship Circles for Youth: Create mentorship programs pairing youth from marginalized groups with local professionals, tradespeople, and artists to build networks, career pathways, apprenticeships, and confidence to stay or return home.
Address: 5945 Spring Garden Road, Unit 101, Halifax, NS B3H 4R4

Description: Eyelevel presents exhibitions, pop-ups, and neighborhood arts events and regularly issues paid calls and microgrants that prioritize Mi’kmaq and other Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, 2SLGBTQ+, and disabled artists. By directing small grants and presentation platforms to equity-deserving creators and hosting free or low-cost programs in accessible spaces, Eyelevel advances inclusive local festivals that foster cross-cultural connections.
Solution: Local Inclusive Festivals and Arts Grants: Sponsor neighborhood festivals and small grants that prioritize programming by Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, 2SLGBTQ+, and disabled artists to celebrate diversity and create cross-cultural engagement.

Description: Mi’kmaw Kina’matnewey supports Mi’kmaw language revitalization through curriculum development, teacher training, community classes, and digital resources used across Nova Scotia’s Mi’kmaw communities. These efforts strengthen access to Mi’kmaw language learning for youth and adults while fostering cross-cultural understanding between Indigenous and newcomer communities.
Solution: Community Language and Interpretation Networks: Organize volunteer interpreter pools and community language classes (including Mi'kmaq language learning support) to lower communication barriers for newcomers and strengthen cross-cultural exchange.

Program: The WorkBridge (Nova Scotia Works for Persons with Disabilities)
Description: The WorkBridge provides tailored employment services for people with disabilities, including career counseling, resume and cover-letter support, interview preparation, and job development. Staff collaborate with clients and employers on accommodation planning and coordinate assistive technology trials through community partners to ensure successful onboarding and retention. The program also hosts employer engagement events and roundtables to connect inclusive employers with talent and share b...
Solution: Disability Employment Support and Skills Labs: Host community-run skills labs offering resume help, workplace accommodation planning, assistive tech demos, and employer roundtables to improve hiring and retention of people with disabilities.
Address: 7051 Bayers Road, Suite 501, Halifax, NS B3L 4V2

Description: ILNS Employment Services offers skills labs and workshops focused on resume building, interview practice, job search strategies, and workplace readiness for persons with disabilities. The team supports individualized accommodation planning and provides orientations to assistive technologies (such as speech-to-text, screen readers, and accessible productivity tools) in their resource space. ILNS also conducts employer outreach, information sessions, and roundtables to advance inclusive hiring ...
Solution: Disability Employment Support and Skills Labs: Host community-run skills labs offering resume help, workplace accommodation planning, assistive tech demos, and employer roundtables to improve hiring and retention of people with disabilities.
Address: 4 Duke Street, Suite 104, Bedford, NS B4A 2Z7

Program: New Leaf Enterprises (Employment and Skills Development)
Description: New Leaf Enterprises provides hands-on skills labs (such as food service, production, and social enterprise work) alongside resume support, job readiness training, and coaching for adults with disabilities. Staff work directly with employers on job carving and accommodation planning, and they familiarize participants and workplaces with adaptive tools used in training to support on-the-job success. The program regularly invites employers for tours and discussion sessions to build inclusive hi...
Solution: Disability Employment Support and Skills Labs: Host community-run skills labs offering resume help, workplace accommodation planning, assistive tech demos, and employer roundtables to improve hiring and retention of people with disabilities.

Description: The Nova Scotia Restorative Justice Program diverts youth and eligible adult matters from the formal justice system into community-based restorative processes. Community justice agencies across the province recruit and train volunteer facilitators to run restorative circles, conferences, and mediations that address harms, including interpersonal discrimination, support accountability, and rebuild relationships. This non-punitive approach centers those affected, encourages dialogue, and connec...
Solution: Neighbourhood Restorative Justice and Conflict Resolution: Set up restorative circles and mediation services facilitated by trained community volunteers to address interpersonal discrimination incidents and rebuild trust without defaulting to punitive systems.

Program: Nova Scotia RCMP – Hate/Bias Incident Reporting and Response
Organization: Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Nova Scotia (H Division)
Description: The Nova Scotia RCMP accepts reports of hate-motivated incidents across the province and documents them for investigation and trend monitoring, coordinating responses through local detachments. Members work with Victim Services and partner organizations to provide supports, safety planning, and referrals, helping affected individuals while liaising with community stakeholders to prevent further harm.
Solution: Bias Incident Reporting and Rapid Response Network: Create a community-managed reporting tool and volunteer rapid-response teams that document incidents, offer supports to affected people, and coordinate with service providers to prevent escalation.

Program: Access to Justice and Human Rights Support
Description: reachAbility runs free legal clinics and advocacy services where people facing discrimination and accessibility barriers can report incidents, have them documented, and receive rapid legal information and support. With volunteer lawyers and advocates, the program assists with human rights complaints, accommodations, and coordinated problem-solving with service providers to reduce conflict and prevent escalation.
Solution: Bias Incident Reporting and Rapid Response Network: Create a community-managed reporting tool and volunteer rapid-response teams that document incidents, offer supports to affected people, and coordinate with service providers to prevent escalation.

Description: Nikani Awtiken is a land-based leadership program where Mi’kmaq Elders and Knowledge Keepers mentor Indigenous youth through cultural teachings, Mi’kmaw language, traditional ecological knowledge, and leadership development. Youth learn hands-on skills (e.g., canoeing, plant medicines, crafts) while building identity, confidence, and community belonging through direct intergenerational exchange.
Solution: Elder–Youth Knowledge Exchanges: Facilitate programs where Mi'kmaq elders, African Nova Scotian storytellers, and community elders mentor youth—sharing cultural practices, local history, trades skills, and leadership development to strengthen belonging.

Organization: Association of Black Social Workers (Nova Scotia)
Description: The Rites of Passage program pairs African Nova Scotian youth with community Elders and storytellers using an Africentric framework to teach cultural history, identity, life skills, and leadership. Through circles, workshops, and mentorship, youth gain guidance from respected community members, strengthening belonging and resilience against racism while exploring education, trades, and career pathways.
Solution: Elder–Youth Knowledge Exchanges: Facilitate programs where Mi'kmaq elders, African Nova Scotian storytellers, and community elders mentor youth—sharing cultural practices, local history, trades skills, and leadership development to strengthen belonging.
Address: 6406 Quinpool Road, Suite 201, Halifax, NS B3L 1A8

Program: Peer-Led Drop-in and Harm Reduction Mental Health Supports
Description: Stepping Stone’s sex worker–led drop-in offers trauma-informed, judgment-free peer support where trained peer staff and volunteers provide mental health check-ins, crisis de-escalation, and navigation to counselling, health, and community resources. The space is intentionally low-barrier and culturally safer for people who experience discrimination, including 2SLGBTQ+, Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, migrant, and disabled community members.
Solution: Community Mental Health Peer Support Network: Train peer-support volunteers from diverse backgrounds to provide culturally safe mental-health drop-in hours, referral navigation, and trauma-informed support for people facing discrimination.

Description: The Municipality of Cumberland partners with private ISPs and neighbouring communities to co‑fund fibre and fixed‑wireless builds in sparsely populated areas. The initiative aggregates local demand, applies for provincial/federal broadband grants, and negotiates bulk build and service terms, enabling affordable last‑mile upgrades that bring reliable high‑speed internet to rural residents and businesses.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Community Broadband Partnerships: Form local consortia (municipalities, businesses, co‑ops) to co‑fund last‑mile broadband upgrades, apply for provincial/federal grants, and negotiate bulk service agreements to improve internet access across rural areas.
Address: 1395 Blair Lake Road, Upper Nappan, NS B4H 3Y4

Description: Canadian Blood Services runs mobile donor clinics that regularly travel to community centres and arenas throughout rural Nova Scotia, bringing the full blood donation experience outside Halifax. These pop-up clinics follow a rotating calendar and provide on-site screening, donation, and post-donation care, enabling residents in smaller communities to participate without long-distance travel.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Mobile Service Units: Operate mobile buses or pop‑up clinics that deliver services (health screenings, mental health supports, library services, business advising, skills training) on a rotating schedule to smaller communities.
Address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 130, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

Program: Secondary and Garden Suites (Accessory Dwelling Units)
Description: The Town of Kentville permits secondary and garden suites (ADUs) in residential areas, providing homeowners with a clear pathway to add small rental units. By supporting gentle-density and infill, the initiative increases affordable options for young people and newcomers in a rural town setting while using existing infrastructure efficiently.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Affordable and Flexible Housing Initiatives: Repurpose vacant buildings, support secondary suites and co‑housing projects, and offer renovation grants or tax incentives for landlords to expand affordable, youth‑friendly housing options.

Program: In.Business: A Mentorship Program for Indigenous Youth (Atlantic Region)
Organization: Cape Breton University – Shannon School of Business
Description: In.Business connects Indigenous high school students with Indigenous business mentors through a blend of in-person events and virtual mentorship led from Cape Breton University. The program nurtures entrepreneurial skills, career exploration, and community-rooted pathways that encourage participants to pursue education, start ventures, and build careers in their home communities across Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Youth Engagement and Return‑Home Campaigns: Run local mentoring, internships, and career‑shadowing programs plus targeted marketing and relocation supports to encourage young people to stay, return, or start businesses in their home communities.
Address: 1250 Grand Lake Road, Sydney, NS B1M 1A2

Program: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts – Community Arts and Festivals
Organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
Description: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts operates a rural arts campus that hosts festivals, exhibitions, outdoor performances, and community arts events that activate public spaces in the Annapolis Valley. Through youth camps, mentorships, and production opportunities with partners, the Centre creates pathways into the creative economy while drawing visitors to a rural cultural hub and strengthening local identity.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Place‑Making and Cultural Activation: Invest in festivals, public art, performance spaces and markets to boost local identity, attract visitors and create creative economy pathways for youth in the arts and culture sectors.
Address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

Program: Ship's Company Theatre – Summer Festival and Waterfront Performance Space
Description: Ship's Company Theatre presents a summer festival of new and established works in a signature waterfront performance space that anchors Parrsboro’s cultural life. The theatre attracts visitors to the Fundy coast, offers youth and emerging artist programming, and stimulates downtown businesses—demonstrating place‑making through live performance, community events, and creative employment in a rural setting.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Place‑Making and Cultural Activation: Invest in festivals, public art, performance spaces and markets to boost local identity, attract visitors and create creative economy pathways for youth in the arts and culture sectors.
Address: 18 Lower Main Street, Parrsboro, NS B0M 1S0

Program: King’s Theatre – Performing Arts and Community Presentations
Description: King’s Theatre is a historic venue in Annapolis Royal that programs film, music, theatre, and community events year‑round, animating the town’s main street and waterfront. By presenting local and touring artists, providing youth workshops and volunteer opportunities, and partnering with community groups, it builds cultural identity, draws cultural tourism, and creates on‑ramps to arts employment in a rural area.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Place‑Making and Cultural Activation: Invest in festivals, public art, performance spaces and markets to boost local identity, attract visitors and create creative economy pathways for youth in the arts and culture sectors.
Address: 209 St George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

Organization: CBDC NOBL (Northern Opportunities for Business Limited)
Description: CBDC NOBL’s CAS program gives rural micro and small businesses subsidized access to professional consultants for bookkeeping/accounting systems, human resources policies and recruitment, procurement readiness, and digital marketing/e‑commerce. By centralizing specialized expertise and making it affordable, CAS lets firms plug into back‑office functions they cannot staff in‑house, helping them scale without duplicating costly infrastructure.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Shared Service Centers for Small Businesses: Provide centralized back‑office supports (accounting, HR, procurement, online sales support) so micro and small rural businesses can scale without duplicating costly infrastructure.
Address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

Program: Deanery Community Kitchen and Food Lab
Description: The Deanery Project offers a licensed, affordable community kitchen and food lab that local producers and startups can rent to develop, test, and package value‑added foods. Through shared equipment, training, and events that connect makers to markets, the facility strengthens the Eastern Shore’s local food economy and creates pathways for rural entrepreneurs outside HRM.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Local Food and Value‑Added Processing: Support community kitchens, shared processing facilities and cooperative marketing for farmers and fishers to add value locally, increase year‑round jobs and create new exportable products.
Address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

Organization: Home of the Guardian Angel (Chebucto Family Centre)
Description: Chebucto Family Centre supports parent-led, cooperative playgroups where caregivers rotate volunteer supervision and share responsibilities, lowering childcare costs for families. The centre provides space, coordination, and resources so parents can attend training, employment supports, and appointments—creating flexible, community-run childcare options that align with the volunteer childcare cooperative model.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Volunteer Childcare Cooperatives: Organize parent‑run or cooperative childcare hubs that reduce costs and increase flexible childcare options, enabling parents and youth to pursue training and work locally.

Description: Owned by the Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA) — a partnership of the Towns of Antigonish, Berwick, and Mahone Bay — the Ellershouse Wind Farm supplies renewable electricity to their community-owned utilities. The project creates local operations and maintenance jobs, lowers power costs for residents served by the municipal utilities, and keeps energy revenues within the towns, enabling reinvestment in community services and local infrastructure.
Challenge: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
Solution: Community Energy and Climate Projects: Develop small‑scale renewable projects (solar co‑ops, biomass) that create local jobs, lower energy costs and generate revenue that can be reinvested in community services.
Address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

Description: A community studio and sewing lounge that transforms a Main Street storefront into shared creative workspace with sewing machines, cutting tables, and craft tools. It offers affordable drop-in bench time, classes, and collaborative projects, giving makers and artists low-cost access to equipment and a supportive, community-managed environment.
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
Solution: Shared Creative Spaces and Maker Hubs: Convert underused rooms, storefronts, or municipal buildings into low-cost shared studios and maker spaces with pooled tools and bench time. Managed by community boards, these hubs offer affordable workspace, equipment access, and meeting space for collaborations.

Description: This annual festival transforms downtown Sydney and surrounding communities with pop-up galleries, performances, and installations in storefronts, parks, and other public spaces—often reanimating vacant or unconventional locations for one night and related events. By dispersing programming across rotating sites, Lumière creates accessible, temporary venues that spotlight emerging and established artists without long-term overhead.
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
Solution: Pop-up and Mobile Venues: Organize short-term pop-up theatres, galleries, and performance stages using vacant storefronts, community centres, parks, and trailers. Rotate locations to activate neighbourhoods, reduce venue scarcity, and give emerging artists exposure without long-term overhead.

Description: An artist cooperative in Pictou showcasing work by member artists from northeastern Nova Scotia. Members pay annual fees, staff the gallery, and pool resources for rent, marketing, and administration, while shared sales commissions and rotating exhibitions sustain operations and keep regional art visible and affordable for the community.
Challenge: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation

Solution: Volunteer Co-op and Shift-Sharing: Form a cooperative of nearby nonprofits and community groups to share volunteers, coordinate schedules, and rotate responsibilities so individuals can contribute without burnout and organizations cover core hours without over-reliance on a few people.
Address: 46 Portland Street, Suite 100, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1H4

Description: Radstorm Halifax operates a working-member program where people contribute set volunteer hours toward tasks like event support, studio maintenance, and mentorship/skill-shares, and in return receive access to its community-run resources (music venue, rehearsal rooms, screenprinting studio, zine library). This is a practical time-credit model that swaps hours for services and space, spreading workloads across many contributors and building a sustainable, peer-supported arts and community hub.
Solution: Local Time Bank / Skills Exchange: Set up a time-banking system where community members earn credits by helping with events, mentorship, or repairs and spend credits on services (childcare, tutoring, tech help), increasing reciprocity and reducing volunteer pressure.

Description: IWK Health’s Volunteer Resources supports volunteers across women’s and children’s health programs with role-specific training, scheduled check-ins with coordinators, and access to debriefing and psychosocial supports after difficult patient encounters. The program emphasizes flexible shift options and respite coverage to prevent overload, and it recognizes volunteer contributions through appreciation activities to encourage long-term retention.
Solution: Community Volunteer Wellness Program: Implement supports for volunteers including regular check-ins, debrief groups, mental-health resources, small appreciation stipends, and respite slots to prevent burnout and retain long-term contributors.

Program: SMUSA Society Funding and Project Grants
Description: Saint Mary’s University Students’ Association allocates part of its student fee revenue to a student-run funding program that awards small grants to student societies and youth-led projects. A committee of student peers evaluates applications and distributes funds, providing a youth-jury model that empowers emerging leaders and supports relevant services and events that keep students engaged locally.
Solution: Youth-Led Mini-Grants and Project Funds: Allocate a portion of community funds to youth juries that select and manage small grants for projects by and for young people, boosting leadership, relevance of services, and youth investment in staying local.

Program: ASU Society Funding and Initiatives Grants
Description: The Acadia Students’ Union administers student-fee–supported grants that fund youth-led societies and projects benefiting students and the broader Wolfville community. Funding decisions are made by student committees, creating a youth-led mini-grant process that develops leadership skills, sustains student-centered services, and encourages young people to build community where they study and live.
Solution: Youth-Led Mini-Grants and Project Funds: Allocate a portion of community funds to youth juries that select and manage small grants for projects by and for young people, boosting leadership, relevance of services, and youth investment in staying local.

Program: Corporate and Group Volunteering & In‑Kind Giving
Description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank engages local employers in organized volunteer days to sort food, refurbish furniture, and support warehouse operations, while also coordinating in‑kind donations of goods and services. Businesses provide pro bono expertise (e.g., logistics, marketing, IT) and sponsorships that bolster infrastructure and program delivery. These partnerships directly expand Parker Street’s capacity to serve low‑income residents and reduce strain on community‑service nonprofits.
Solution: Business–Community Partnership Network: Organize a local employer network for in-kind support, payroll-giving, pro bono services, employee volunteer days, and sponsorship of capacity-building efforts for nonprofits.

Description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank conducts online crowdfunding appeals using personal stories from clients and volunteers to motivate grassroots giving. At intervals, local businesses sponsor matching gifts (“double your impact”) that multiply small donations and bring visibility and resources to underfunded emergency food, heat, and furniture assistance programs.
Solution: Local Crowdfunding and Storytelling Campaigns: Run community crowdfunding drives that pair personal stories with small matching gifts from local businesses to mobilize resident giving and spotlight underfunded programs.

Description: An annual community fundraising broadcast that shares powerful patient and family stories from across Atlantic Canada to inspire broad-based, small-donor giving. Local businesses and media partners provide sponsorships and matching gift segments, turning personal storytelling into community crowdfunding that supports underfunded pediatric care and family programs at the IWK.
Solution: Local Crowdfunding and Storytelling Campaigns: Run community crowdfunding drives that pair personal stories with small matching gifts from local businesses to mobilize resident giving and spotlight underfunded programs.
Address: 5855 Spring Garden Road, Suite 302, Halifax, NS B3H 4N1

Program: Family Leadership Council (FLC) – Volunteer Caregiver Advisors
Description: IWK Health’s Family Leadership Council is composed of volunteer caregiver advisors who co-design programs and services for women, children, and youth. The council reduces barriers to participation by covering practical expenses like on-site parking and reimbursing or arranging childcare and transit support for meetings and working groups.
Solution: Childcare and Transportation Stipends for Volunteers: Offer small stipends or vouchers to cover childcare, transit, or parking for volunteers—especially younger people and caregivers—to remove practical barriers to participation.

Program: QEII Health Sciences Centre – Volunteer Services
Organization: Nova Scotia Health (QEII Health Sciences Centre)
Description: Volunteer Services at the QEII supports hundreds of volunteers in clinical and non-clinical roles. To lower the cost of volunteering, the program provides free or reimbursed parking when on duty, offers transit ticket support where needed, and reimburses mileage for approved off-site roles, enabling participation by students, young adults, and caregivers without adding transportation costs.
Solution: Childcare and Transportation Stipends for Volunteers: Offer small stipends or vouchers to cover childcare, transit, or parking for volunteers—especially younger people and caregivers—to remove practical barriers to participation.

Organization: Government of Nova Scotia — Communities, Culture, Tourism and Heritage
Description: The Province of Nova Scotia hosts an annual Provincial Volunteer Awards ceremony during National Volunteer Week that brings together municipalities, nonprofits, and residents to celebrate exceptional community service. As a province‑wide recognition festival with networking and engagement opportunities, it helps elevate a culture of giving and volunteerism and complements local recruitment and donor activities that many communities organize around the event.
Solution: Annual Community Giving and Volunteer Festivals: Organize yearly festivals that combine volunteer recruitment, donor drives, recognition ceremonies, and mini-grants to energize philanthropy and celebrate community contributions.

Description: CKDU 88.1 FM is Halifax’s campus-community radio station where volunteers produce local programming that spotlights Nova Scotian entrepreneurs, artists, tradespeople, and community leaders. Through interviews, features, and podcasts distributed on-air and online, CKDU trains new storytellers and amplifies success narratives from across the province. The station also supports live remote broadcasts and occasional listening events, bringing community stories directly to audiences.
Solution: Community Storytelling Campaign: Collect and amplify local success stories (entrepreneurs, artists, tradespeople, returnees) through short videos, podcasts, social posts and local media to reshape narratives about opportunity and quality of life. Volunteer storytellers, schools, and community media can produce content and host listening events.

Description: Acadia’s alumni chapters in Toronto, Calgary, Ottawa, and beyond host events and webinars that spotlight Nova Scotia career paths, entrepreneurship in the Annapolis Valley, and ways alumni can plug into the regional ecosystem. Its mentoring platform and volunteer network create warm introductions for returnees, encourage alumni engagement with the Acadia Entrepreneurship Centre and local ventures, and share relocation and remote-work resources for those looking to move back or stay connected ...
Solution: Alumni & Diaspora Engagement: Create local chapters and events for Nova Scotian alumni and diaspora to connect with hometown opportunities—mentoring, investment clubs, returnee recruitment drives and remote-work relocation supports.

Description: Devour! is an annual festival in Wolfville that blends film, food, and culture, showcasing Nova Scotia’s chefs, producers, and culinary traditions alongside international programming. It implements the solution through pop-up dinners, tasting tours, workshops, and screenings that highlight local talent and lifestyle, drawing visitors and media attention to the province’s vibrant food scene.
Solution: Cultural Festivals & Creative Showcases: Expand and promote festivals and arts events that highlight local culture, talent and lifestyle—run volunteer-led pop-up concerts, gallery nights, food trails and heritage tours to attract visitors and media.

Description: Festival Antigonish presents a summer season of professional theatre at the Bauer Theatre, featuring local and regional artists, community engagement, and special events. By staging accessible performances, talkbacks, and creative showcases, the festival amplifies Nova Scotia’s cultural life and attracts visitors to the region, strengthening the province’s contemporary arts brand.
Solution: Cultural Festivals & Creative Showcases: Expand and promote festivals and arts events that highlight local culture, talent and lifestyle—run volunteer-led pop-up concerts, gallery nights, food trails and heritage tours to attract visitors and media.

Program: Halifax Citadel Ghost Tours and Living History
Description: The Halifax Citadel Society offers seasonal ghost tours, guided heritage experiences, and costumed living-history demonstrations at the national historic site. These heritage tours showcase local stories and culture in immersive, media-friendly formats, drawing audiences to downtown Halifax and reinforcing Nova Scotia’s identity as a place rich in history and unique experiences.
Solution: Cultural Festivals & Creative Showcases: Expand and promote festivals and arts events that highlight local culture, talent and lifestyle—run volunteer-led pop-up concerts, gallery nights, food trails and heritage tours to attract visitors and media.

Organization: Halifax International Airport Authority (Halifax Stanfield International Airport)
Description: Halifax Stanfield’s Tartan Team trains community volunteers to warmly welcome arriving travelers, guide them through the airport, and offer local advice on what to see and do. As first-point hosts for visiting media, investors, students, and job candidates, these volunteers provide authentic hospitality and introductions that positively shape perceptions of Nova Scotia.
Solution: Neighbourhood Hospitality & Host Programs: Train volunteers from across the community to serve as 'hosts' for visiting journalists, prospective investors, students and job candidates—offering authentic local tours, introductions and hospitality that change perceptions.

Program: CBDC NOBL – Small Business Financing and Self‑Employment Supports
Description: CBDC NOBL provides community-sourced loans, self-employment benefits, and advisory services to startups and returning entrepreneurs across northern Nova Scotia, leveraging federal (ACOA), municipal, and local business partnerships. By matching entrepreneurs with accessible capital and layered supports—including referrals to local grants and mentorship—it reduces upfront costs and risk for newcomers and returnees starting or expanding small businesses.
Solution: Welcome-to-Work & Return Incentive Matchmaking: Coordinate community-funded matching incentives (relocation grants, childcare subsidies, small business startup supports) sourced from local businesses, foundations and municipalities to lower barriers for new hires and returnees.
Address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

Program: EHS Nova Scotia Paramedic Tuition Reimbursement (Return-of-Service) Program
Organization: Emergency Medical Care Inc. (EHS Nova Scotia)
Description: Emergency Medical Care Inc. (operating EHS Nova Scotia) offers tuition reimbursement to paramedic students and new graduates who agree to a multi‑year return-of-service working with EHS in Nova Scotia. The reimbursement reduces student loan principal and education costs, while the contractual service term keeps early-career clinicians living and working in local communities. This aligns with the solution by converting community-backed funding into direct debt relief tied to regional retention.
Solution: Community Student Debt Relief Fund: A pooled fund run by the community foundation and local donors that provides targeted principal paydowns or grants for young residents who commit to living and working in the region for a set period (e.g., 3–5 years). This directly lowers debt burden and incentivizes staying/returning.
Address: 239 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 2B2

Program: Physician Recruitment and Retention Incentive Program
Organization: Municipality of the County of Cumberland
Description: The Municipality of the County of Cumberland provides grants and financial incentives, including education debt support, to medical residents and physicians who sign return-of-service agreements to practice in the county for multiple years. These community-funded incentives directly reduce debt burdens for young professionals while binding recipients to live and work locally, strengthening long-term retention. Description: The Yarmouth Hospital Foundation offers community-donor–funded bursaries to students in health disciplines who commit to return‑of‑service in the Tri‑County/Yarmouth region after graduation. These awards reduce upfront education costs and student debt while requiring recipients to practice locally for a set period, directly encouraging them to live and work in the area. By pairing targeted grants with service commitments, the program advances the solution’s aim of debt relief tied to regional...
Solution: Community Student Debt Relief Fund: A pooled fund run by the community foundation and local donors that provides targeted principal paydowns or grants for young residents who commit to living and working in the region for a set period (e.g., 3–5 years). This directly lowers debt burden and incentivizes staying/returning.

Program: Affordable Homeownership Program – South Shore Chapter
Organization: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia – South Shore Chapter
Description: Through its South Shore Chapter, Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia delivers the same shared-equity homeownership model in Lunenburg County, purchasing or servicing land and constructing homes sold with an affordable first mortgage and a deferred shared-equity second mortgage. The model reduces down payment barriers and overall mortgage costs for local families while embedding resale conditions that maintain affordability for future buyers.
Solution: Shared-Equity Homeownership (Community Land Trust): A community land trust purchases land and sells homes with shared-equity arrangements so young buyers need smaller down payments and lower mortgage costs while stewarding long-term affordability in neighbourhoods.

Description: Eskasoni First Nation’s Housing Department administers CMHC Section 95 homes using a rent‑to‑own policy, where monthly occupancy payments are credited toward eventual transfer of ownership after the amortization term. This structure reduces upfront down‑payment barriers and converts housing payments into equity, helping young band members with student debt build wealth and stay employed locally. The community-led model keeps ownership rooted in Eskasoni while creating long‑term affordability.
Solution: Rent-to-Own Cooperative Housing: Local housing co-ops create rent-to-own units where a portion of monthly rent is credited toward future purchase, enabling young households to build equity while staying locally employed.
Address: 63 Mini Mall Drive, Eskasoni, NS B1W 1A1

Description: Millbrook First Nation’s Housing Department provides a rent‑to‑own pathway for CMHC Section 95 units, applying a portion of monthly payments toward the eventual purchase of the home. By transforming rent into equity over a fixed term, the program enables younger households—often carrying student debt—to secure ownership without a large down payment, maintaining ties to local employment and community. The initiative embeds long‑term affordability and community stewardship of housing.
Solution: Rent-to-Own Cooperative Housing: Local housing co-ops create rent-to-own units where a portion of monthly rent is credited toward future purchase, enabling young households to build equity while staying locally employed.

Description: St. Martha’s Regional Hospital Foundation supports current and prospective Nova Scotia Health staff with education and tuition assistance tied to return‑of‑service in the Antigonish area. The fund is coordinated with departmental training budgets at the employer (Nova Scotia Health) so that foundation dollars match or supplement employer tuition-repayment/education support, lowering debt barriers for recruits and upskilling local staff in high‑need roles.
Solution: Employer–Community Tuition Repayment Network: A coalition where local employers offer partial tuition-repayment or loan-assistance packages for staff, with community foundations or municipalities providing matching contributions to amplify impact.

Description: The Cape Breton Regional Hospital Foundation offers bursaries and tuition assistance to healthcare learners and employees who commit to work with Nova Scotia Health in Cape Breton. By aligning foundation funding with employer recruitment and education supports—and, where applicable, community recruitment efforts—the program functions as a local employer–community tuition‑repayment network that reduces debt loads and improves retention.
Solution: Employer–Community Tuition Repayment Network: A coalition where local employers offer partial tuition-repayment or loan-assistance packages for staff, with community foundations or municipalities providing matching contributions to amplify impact.

Organization: Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency, Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration (Government of Nova Scotia)
Description: The START Program provides employers with wage incentives and milestone payments to hire and retain apprentices and other job seekers in Nova Scotia. Employers commit to mentoring and on-the-job training while the program offsets a portion of wages and supports retention through completion bonuses, reducing the financial burden of training and helping young people build careers without relocating.
Solution: Apprenticeship Wage Top-Up and Retention Support: Local businesses and trade associations pool funds to top up apprentice and entry-level wages, provide mentoring, and reduce the financial penalty of training so young people can build careers without moving away.

Program: Credit Counselling and Debt Management Program (Halifax)
Organization: Credit Counselling Services of Atlantic Canada, Inc.
Description: Credit Counselling Services of Atlantic Canada provides free, confidential one-on-one credit counselling and budgeting support to help individuals assess student loans and unsecured debt, create repayment plans, and explore consolidation or refinancing options. They also host community information sessions in Halifax and across Nova Scotia, guiding young people through budgeting strategies aligned with local housing costs and regional career paths.
Solution: Community Debt Coaching and Refinance Clinics: Volunteer-run clinics and one-on-one financial coaching hosted by nonprofit groups and credit unions to help young people explore refinancing, consolidation, repayment plans, and budgeting strategies tailored to regional housing and career paths.
Address: 610-5991 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3H 1Y6

Program: CPA Canada Financial Literacy Program (Nova Scotia)
Organization: CPA Nova Scotia (in partnership with CPA Canada)
Description: Volunteer Chartered Professional Accountants deliver free workshops and clinics on budgeting, managing debt, and understanding credit at libraries, campuses, and community centres throughout Nova Scotia. Sessions often include one-on-one Q&A and coaching, helping young adults evaluate student-loan repayment strategies, consolidation options, and budgeting approaches tailored to the local job market and cost of living.
Solution: Community Debt Coaching and Refinance Clinics: Volunteer-run clinics and one-on-one financial coaching hosted by nonprofit groups and credit unions to help young people explore refinancing, consolidation, repayment plans, and budgeting strategies tailored to regional housing and career paths.

Program: Financial Literacy and Money Management for Newcomers
Organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
Description: ISANS offers workshops and individualized coaching on budgeting, banking, credit building, and debt management for newcomers, including youth and recent graduates. Staff and partner volunteers help participants understand student loans, evaluate consolidation/refinancing options with local credit unions and banks, and plan repayments that reflect Nova Scotia’s housing market and employment landscape.
Solution: Community Debt Coaching and Refinance Clinics: Volunteer-run clinics and one-on-one financial coaching hosted by nonprofit groups and credit unions to help young people explore refinancing, consolidation, repayment plans, and budgeting strategies tailored to regional housing and career paths.

Organization: Dalhousie University – Office of Advancement (Alumni Engagement)
Description: Dal Alumni Link pairs students and recent graduates with alumni mentors in Nova Scotia for one-to-one guidance, career navigation, and warm introductions into local industries. By organizing structured mentor-matching and alumni-hosted networking, it strengthens the support circles that help new grads build careers and stay rooted in the province.
Solution: Alumni Sponsorship and Mentorship Circles: Local university and college alumni clubs organize sponsorships, emergency loan pools, mentor-matching and short-term grants for graduates who choose to live/work locally, combining financial help with career support.

Organization: Nova Scotia Community College – Alumni Relations
Description: NSCC Alumni Connect is a province-wide online platform that matches recent graduates with alumni mentors for advice, referrals, and career support in Nova Scotia’s communities and industries. Alumni chapters and volunteers also sponsor local meetups and panels, combining mentor-matching with practical sponsorship of opportunities that help grads establish themselves locally.
Solution: Alumni Sponsorship and Mentorship Circles: Local university and college alumni clubs organize sponsorships, emergency loan pools, mentor-matching and short-term grants for graduates who choose to live/work locally, combining financial help with career support.

Description: Saint Mary’s University’s Ten Thousand Coffees platform connects students and recent graduates with alumni for career conversations, job shadowing, and introductions within Halifax’s business and nonprofit communities. Alumni sponsors use the network to surface internships and early-career roles, implementing the mentor-matching and sponsorship elements that encourage graduates to stay and grow in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Alumni Sponsorship and Mentorship Circles: Local university and college alumni clubs organize sponsorships, emergency loan pools, mentor-matching and short-term grants for graduates who choose to live/work locally, combining financial help with career support.

Description: Delivered by Acadia Entrepreneurship Centre, the SEB program provides eligible new founders—including recent graduates—with income support and intensive business coaching while they start a company in the Annapolis Valley. Drawing on Acadia’s mentor network (including alumni advisors), it blends financial assistance with mentorship to help graduates root their enterprises in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Alumni Sponsorship and Mentorship Circles: Local university and college alumni clubs organize sponsorships, emergency loan pools, mentor-matching and short-term grants for graduates who choose to live/work locally, combining financial help with career support.

Description: Navigate provides a coworking space with reliable high-speed internet, desks, and meeting facilities in Sydney, alongside coaching, mentorship, and regular skills and employer-connection events. By helping entrepreneurs, freelancers, and grads plug into remote-friendly opportunities and networks while staying in Cape Breton, it advances higher-earning pathways that ease student debt pressures without requiring relocation.
Solution: Shared Workspaces and Remote-Job Hubs: Community-operated coworking hubs with high-speed internet, mentoring and job placement services let residents access higher-paying remote work without relocating, improving incomes while keeping roots local.

Description: LaunchBox is a university-affiliated coworking and startup hub that offers high-speed internet, shared workspace, mentorship, and experiential training for students and recent graduates in the Annapolis Valley. Its programming connects participants with remote-ready skills, advisors, and employer and investor networks so they can access remote roles or build location-independent ventures in Nova Scotia, supporting income growth while remaining local.
Solution: Shared Workspaces and Remote-Job Hubs: Community-operated coworking hubs with high-speed internet, mentoring and job placement services let residents access higher-paying remote work without relocating, improving incomes while keeping roots local.

Program: Town of Amherst – Physician Recruitment and Retention Incentive
Description: The Town of Amherst provides financial incentives and relocation assistance to recruit and retain physicians, with support from municipal funds and local community partners. These incentives operate like welcome grants that can be used for moving expenses, initial housing needs, and other start-up costs—particularly valuable for Nova Scotians returning after medical education or residency outside the province.
Solution: Return-to-Community Welcome Grants: Small cash grants or relocation bonuses funded by municipalities, community foundations and local businesses for people who return to Nova Scotia after completing education elsewhere, used for housing deposits, moving costs or startup expenses.
Address: 98 Victoria Street East, Amherst, NS B4H 1X6

Program: Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) – Nova Scotia Student Assistance
Organization: Nova Scotia Student Assistance (Government of Nova Scotia)
Description: RAP lets Nova Scotians repay student loans based on their actual income, with payments reduced or paused when earnings are low and government covering the difference. By tying repayment to income earned in local jobs rather than fixed schedules, it implements the solution’s core mechanism of income-contingent, time-limited repayment and reduces upfront financial pressure that can drive graduates to leave the province.
Solution: Community Income Share Agreement (ISA) Pool: A locally governed ISA program where community investors fund education or training for residents in exchange for modest, time-limited income shares, aligning repayment with local job prospects and reducing upfront debt.
Address: 2021 Brunswick Street, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 2S9

Program: Nursing Education Tuition Relief and Return-of-Service Incentives
Organization: Nova Scotia Department of Health and Wellness / Nova Scotia Health
Description: Nova Scotia funds portions of nursing education and offers grants in exchange for a time-limited return-of-service in provincial health care. This shifts costs from upfront tuition to an obligation tied to local employment and earnings, echoing a community ISA by aligning “repayment” with working in Nova Scotia and easing debt burdens that might otherwise push graduates to higher-paying markets elsewhere.
Solution: Community Income Share Agreement (ISA) Pool: A locally governed ISA program where community investors fund education or training for residents in exchange for modest, time-limited income shares, aligning repayment with local job prospects and reducing upfront debt.
Address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

Organization: Nova Scotia Health / Nova Scotia Department of Health and Wellness
Description: PRAP-NS supports internationally trained physicians to enter practice in Nova Scotia, with placements that include return-of-service commitments in designated communities. By replacing large upfront costs with a time-bound obligation linked to employment and income in the province, it mirrors the ISA model’s alignment of repayment with local job outcomes, helping retain talent and reduce financial barriers.
Solution: Community Income Share Agreement (ISA) Pool: A locally governed ISA program where community investors fund education or training for residents in exchange for modest, time-limited income shares, aligning repayment with local job prospects and reducing upfront debt.
Address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

Program: More Opportunity for Skilled Trades (MOST) Tax Refund
Organization: Department of Finance and Treasury Board, Government of Nova Scotia
Description: MOST provides an annual refund of provincial income tax paid on the first $50,000 of eligible earnings for qualified workers under 30 in designated occupations. By significantly reducing early-career tax burdens for young residents who live and work in Nova Scotia, it functions as a targeted tax-relief incentive that makes it more affordable to stay and build a life in the province.
Solution: Local Loyalty and Tax-Relief Incentives: Community-led incentive packages—such as discounts from local businesses, property-tax deferral programs run by municipalities, or rebate vouchers from chambers of commerce—help reduce early household costs for young residents committing to stay.
